#5003. Where Does Brock Purdy Live? Exploring the Homes of the San Francisco 49ers Quarterback

He spends plenty of time at Levi Stadium as the quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers, but where does Brock Purdy live when he’s off the field? The football player was born and raised in Queen Creek, Arizona, and played football at Perry High School in nearby Gilbert. While Purdy left Arizona in 2018 to play at Iowa State University, he’s still fond of his home state. “I love the state of Arizona and everyone that’s been a part of my life,” he told reporters ahead of the 2024 Super Bowl. “And obviously, I’m trying to represent them as best as I can for as long as my career goes.”

At Iowa State, Purdy was a three-time All-Big 12 quarterback and was the winningest quarterback in the school’s history. The University’s Midwest environment suited Purdy. “My favorite part is the people, just because of how down-to-earth and real everyone is,” he told the Iowa Stater in 2024. “Everyone wants to help each other out. There’s no selfishness. I don’t know what it is about the culture in Iowa, but everybody just loves one another authentically. And when you go back, you feel that every time.” Purdy also met his future wife, Jenna, his freshman year at Iowa State. The couple got engaged in 2023 and tied the knot back in Iowa in 2024.

In 2022, the San Francisco 49ers selected Purdy as the final pick of the NFL Draft. This pick typically earns the harsh nickname Mr. Irrelevant, but Purdy quickly proved the moniker wrong, becoming starting quarterback in his rookie season. Now in his fifth season with the 49ers, Purdy is also building a successful life off the field. Read on to learn about Brock Purdy’s homes over the years.

Teammates—and onetime roommates—Alfredo Gutierrez, Nick Zakelj, and Purdy in the locker room in 2022

At the beginning of his NFL career, Purdy lived more like a recent college grad than a pro football player. During his rookie year, Purdy shared a house with offensive linemen Alfredo Gutierrez and Nick Zakelj. The trio even gave out a Christmas card from the household to teammates. In an interview with NBC Sports Bay Area, Gutierrez revealed that Purdy did most of the cooking out of the three and that they spent downtime watching football, movies, and playing Mario Super Slugger.

By 2023, Purdy had only one roommate: Zakelj. “So he and I are still splitting rent,” Purdy told the TODAY Show. “I still drive my Toyota Sequoia. Other than that, it’s pretty simple.”

Purdy with his wife, Jenna, and daughter, Millie Joleen, in 2025. They now have a second child on the way.

Purdy left his shared home in 2024 when he married his wife, Jenna. They now live in a rental home in the Bay Area with their daughter, Millie Joleen, who was born in July 2025. The couple announced in July 2026 that they would soon be welcoming a second child.

The couple focused on making the home family-friendly, adding plenty of storage for their daughter’s toys, and durable furniture for hosting. “Becoming new parents, we really wanted this house to feel like a home where our family is going to continue to grow,” Jenna said in a video unveiling the couple’s living room and bedroom makeovers, which they worked on with Pottery Barn.

In May 2025, Purdy signed a five-year, $265 million deal with the 49ers, making him the fifth-highest-paid quarterback in the league. The hefty pay raise led Purdy to start his real estate portfolio. His teammate, 49ers tight end George Kittle, revealed on a podcast in June of that year that Purdy had purchased a home in Nashville.

Purdy with teammate George Kittle in 2025

“He did purchase a house in Nashville, Tennessee,” Kittle said. “He will be kind of a neighbor to me at some point. That will be pretty fun, because I’ll have a quarterback that can throw to me all the time, that’s actually on my team.” That summer, Purdy was seen training at Kittle’s football compound in Nashville.

#5002. Want to Do Less But Get More? This Lash Trend is For You.

If you’ve got thirty seconds, you’ve got plenty of time to make your eyes stand out.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

IT’S QUITE POSSIBLE THAT MASCARA has been the loudest thing on your face for years. And now, there’s a new trend that’s here to turn down the volume. ‘Ghost lashes’ refer to an effort to add a little impact to your fringe without the need for coat after coat of makeup. The idea: Curl, add a single whisper of brown mascara, and let your natural lashes take the lead.

It’s a decidedly different take—especially for someone like me. I wore lash extensions for more than a decade and mastered the at-home versions during the pandemic and beyond. But now,, I’m coming around to skipping mascara (though I’ll keep my tightlining, thank you very much). It’s beauty’s back-to-basics era, lash edition. Fewer products, less fuss, more of what you already have.

My lash drawer can finally, exhilaratingly, let out a deep exhale. “We’ve become so used to seeing a full lash that taking it away suddenly feels...interesting,” says celebrity makeup artist Benjamin Puckey. It tracks with what he’s seeing in the chair: Clients are asking for less mascara and no longer requesting falsies. The payoff reaches well past what’s sprouting from your lids. Leaving lashes bare allows the rest of your face finally gets a turn. “You notice the skin, the shape of the eyes or the lip color differently,” Puckey says.

Meet the experts: Benjamin Puckey is a celebrity makeup artists based in New York City. Tobi Henney is a celebrity makeup artist based in Los Angeles.

Ahead, how to pull it off at home and what to know before you break up with black mascara.

Picture the no-makeup makeup look, but for your eyes. Puckey describes ghost lashes as lashes left bare or wearing so little mascara you barely register it. Curling is fine and a light coat of brown is fine. The thickness, the black pigment and, of course, the falsies are out. Makeup artist Tobi Henney keeps her definition refreshingly short: Ghost lashes are when “you don’t use mascara on the lashes and they are left natural.” She has the red carpet receipts, too. “I did this look in Cannes on Barbara Palvin,” she says. Her styling rule: The rest of your face “has to have stand out elements,” such as a flush of blush or a statement lip, “to carry the look.”

The trend grew out of the no-makeup movement, which started when Pamela Anderson gave up most makeup back in 2019. By 2025, it had trickled down to runways: Valentino’s spring/summer 2025 show and Gucci Cruise 2026 in May 2025 featured bare-lash looks. Then, more young Gen Z TikTok creators started posting clean makeup looks with no mascara, framing it as a recession-proof beauty move. The look spread further as Addison Rae, Kylie Jenner and Hailey Bieber posted bare-lash selfies and became a mainstream summer 2026 trend when Zendaya wore it to The Odyssey premiere.

We love it because it effectively ends the lash arms race. Skip the heavy stuff and your skin, your eye shape and your lip color get to shine. “It allows a little more of the person to come through,” Puckey says. It’s you, only a little more awake.

Another big part of this is the attempt to get your natural lashes to grown on their own, without the visual help of mascara. These days, there are plenty of options, from those that use analogues of prostaglandins (the active ingredient in prescription Latisse, widely considered to be the gold-standard in lash growth) and those without (prostaglandins can be irritating for some and some research shows they may cause color changes to the iris in rare cases). These products typically take several weeks to months to show results, but many can be extremely effective at boosting the length and volume of your natural lashes.

Good news: This routine costs you less time and less money than the one you’re doing now. The trick is to let your lashes be the last thing you think about. Keep your skin light, dab on concealer where you need it, add blush and brush your brows into place. Then work through the steps below.

A bi-phase formula that will remove oils and leftover product so that your lashes are perfectly primed for what’s to come.

The broad curved shape grabs ever last lash, from inner to outer corner, while the flexible silicone pads won’t tug at your fringe.

Deeply pigmented (so you’re going to want to wipe this one on a tissue before applying), but the results are and smudge- and flake-free.

This prostaglandin-free formula is powered with peptides and biotin to lengthen without irritation.

Plenty. A fair warning: Ghost lashes aren’t one-size-fits-all. Puckey says contrast matters. On a low-contrast face, where skin, hair, brows and lashes are close in color, black mascara can become the loudest thing you see, while brown feels more balanced. If you have naturally dark lashes against lighter skin, you may already have plenty of definition. Fair or sparse lashes can make the no-mascara look less appealing if you’re used to a stronger frame around your eyes.

Age may play a part, too. Puckey finds the fully bare version is often easier to wear under 40, though he wouldn’t call it a rule. As lashes get finer or less dense, a little mascara can make a real difference to how defined your eyes look. It’s also important to mind your technique. Puckey says the most common curler mistakes are squeezing too hard, curling over dried mascara and using a worn or damaged pad. Never pull the curler through your lashes while it’s clamped shut.

Then there’s the serum question. Henney is a fan: “I love the Sweed Eyelash Growth Serum, it works wonders,” she says. Her timeline for short or sparse lashes: “You need a few weeks or months to see results.” Puckey takes a different view. You don’t need a serum to try this look, and he wouldn’t start an expensive routine just to make a trend work. He leaves ingredient picks and timelines to a dermatologist or eye doctor. On safety, Henney says to “always check if you have contact lenses,” and Puckey says to ask an eye doctor, especially if you have sensitive eyes or wear contacts. If a product irritates your eyes, stop using it. If your lashes have suddenly gone sparse or patchy, Puckey says to have a dermatologist take a look.

Set your expectations before you start. Ghost lashes read softer and less defined than a full, mascara-heavy lash. A curler can make short lashes more visible, but it can’t create density that isn’t there. If you go the serum route, Henney’s advice is brief: “Be consistent.”

Here’s your homework. Finish your makeup, curl your lashes, then pause before you reach for the mascara. “You might like what you see,” Puckey says. And if you miss the definition, add a little brown. Going fully bare is optional. “There’s no need to follow the idea so literally that you stop feeling like yourself,” Puckey says.

Wear it your way, and you’ve done it right.

#5001. Strategy Resumes Bitcoin Buys With $66M Purchase

Strategy Resumes Bitcoin Buys With $66M Purchase

Strategy bought 811 BTC for $65.5 million last week, the company said on Monday, resuming its Bitcoin purchases after a one-week pause.

The Bitcoin treasury firm paid an average of $80,846 per coin between October 26 and November 1, funding the purchases by selling 1,178,552 shares of MSTR stock for $164 million in net proceeds, according to an SEC filing. Of that, $65.5 million went to Bitcoin and $98.5 million to its USD Cash account.

Strategy has acquired 811 $BTC and repurchased $208M of $STRC. As of 11/1/26, we hold 849,327 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTRhttps://t.co/fk7kWJxf3L

Strategy now holds 849,327 BTC, acquired for a total of $64.08 billion at an average of about $75,451 per coin.

The company also bought back 2,092,035 shares of STRC, its variable-rate preferred stock, for $208.2 million, all paid from USD Cash. That is up from $204.9 million the previous week, when Strategy paused its Bitcoin buying for the first time since mid-September. The week before that, it bought 267 BTC for $22.1 million.

USD Cash, the pool Strategy keeps for general purposes including buying Bitcoin, fell to $132.7 million from $242.4 million a week earlier. Its separate USD Reserve, which covers preferred dividends and interest on its debt, stood at $4.79 billion after paying out $43.4 million in dividends. About $748.6 million remains available under its program for repurchasing preferred stock.

Strategy put its combined USD assets at $4.9 billion and its "USD Duration," its measure of how long those assets could cover dividends and interest, at 3.3 years, it tweeted.

The purchases come as STRC moves to a new dividend schedule. Shareholders approved daily dividends on Strategy's four preferred stocks last week, with STRC's first daily record date falling on November 1.

Mizuho Financial Group maintained its Outperform rating and $165 price target on MSTR following Strategy's third-quarter earnings call, pointing to a stronger balance sheet with net leverage down to 2.4% from 8.4%, according to a summary of the note. But analyst Dan Dolev also flagged dilution concerns, noting that Bitcoin per share has fallen 3.7% this year.

Strategy also faces possible removal from MSCI's equity indexes under a rule the index provider finalized in October, which treats companies dominated by a single asset as ineligible. MSCI will publish the list of affected companies on November 11.

#4998. Morning Minute: Binance Hack Leads to Mass Outflows While FBI Opens Probe

Morning Minute: Binance Hack Leads to Mass Outflows While FBI Opens Probe

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

💸 The Binance Hack Just Cost Bitcoin ETFs Their Whole Month

Through Thursday, October was a quiet, slightly positive month for Bitcoin ETFs. Then North Korea took $6.4 billion out of Binance five minutes after the closing bell, and Friday’s single session erased the entire month.

To recap the Binance hack, attackers drained roughly $6.4 billion from Binance’s hot wallets across about 10 blockchains, with most of it inside 20 minutes on Thursday afternoon. That’s more than four times the old record, the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025. Both firms attribute it to TraderTraitor, the North Korea-linked group that also hit Bybit.

The entry point has changed since Friday. Binance first blamed a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, then found “additional points of breach.” On Ethereum, the attacker used 50 pre-signed authorizations to turn a Binance hot wallet into a contract that emptied itself—a failure of Binance’s own signing approvals, not of Ethereum. No private keys leaked. The attacker wiped its tooling on the way out.

Friday was the aftermath, and it was bloody. Bitcoin ETFs bled $643.3 million on Friday, the biggest day of the month, ending a four-session buying streak. That one day took October from +$127 million to −$515.9 million. September was +$2.65 billion. The ETH ETFs were worse: −$1.61 billion for October, their worst month since launch, and an 11-session losing streak into the weekend.

Now the biggest players in the U.S. government are reacting. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC the hack “proves our exact point.” “The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don’t have the same sorts of safeguards.” He’s pitching a “federal option”—let offshore venues register with the CFTC and meet US cybersecurity standards. He also notes the hole came in “from someone’s laptop,” not from a blockchain. The FBI and Secret Service have also both opened probes.

Binance CEO Richard Teng says the company covers every dollar from corporate funds and SAFU, with $6.34 billion already set aside. CZ: “It hurts, but we survive.” Withdrawals were turned back on over the weekend and over $3.6B has exited so far according to QCP.

So what to watch from here? Monday’s inflows (or outflows) will be telling. If Friday’s bleeding continues to Monday, it’s a signal that the pain might just be beginning. Also, watch Binance. They have to buy roughly $1.3 billion of BTC, ETH, and BNB on the open market and OTC to top off the reimbursement pool—a forced bid underneath a market that just got hit. And then there’s Selig and the FBI; be on the lookout from updates from those agencies as the Binance hack aftermath carries forward.

#4997. How to Kill a Tree Stump, According to Experts—And Why It’s Important for Your Yard’s Health

Removing a tree from your property can be daunting, especially considering you can’t just shout “Timber!” and move on: You might need to know how to kill a tree stump as well. Just as an ailing or overgrown tree may put your roof, patio, or parked cars at risk if limbs start dropping, an untended tree stump may well cause underground damage to pipes or the foundation of your home as its roots keep spreading.

So your upcoming arboreal project may start with tree removal, but it’s important for the health of your lawn and your home to learn how to kill a tree stump in the aftermath. Even if you don’t plan to use the space where the tree once stood, according to the arborists we consulted, a tree stump left just sitting around can cause a host of new problems. While there’s more than one way to remove a tree stump, the consensus is universal: To consider tree removal truly complete, you’ll need to kill a tree stump, too.

“Old stumps attract pests, harbor fungi, and become tripping hazards,” says Melissa Rolston, chief strategy officer at Paramount Landscaping. “Some even try to regrow. Removing them protects your soil, prevents infestation, and keeps your yard design intentional.”

Rolston adds that the pest problem an unattended rotting tree stump causes can spread. Insects like ants and termites that might be drawn to a tempting tree stump can multiply and affect an entire property, potentially damaging healthy plant life directly and/or by spreading fungi or pathogens to nearby trees and plants. That “dead” tree stump may well become the launchpad for invaders that are very much alive—and very harmful to your yard.

Now that we’ve established a few of the reasons why you might need to kill a tree stump, read on to learn about a few methods you can use to get rid of a tree stump for good. Note that if the first approach fails to work on a truly tough tree stump, you can then move on to the second or third technique. If time isn’t a factor (as in, you’re not in a tree-stump removal rush to build a new patio or solarium), then the fourth approach is the least invasive in terms of impact on your property’s ecosystem.

Before you decide which tree stump removal method you’re going with to remove the stump in question, you should figure out how big of a job it is—literally. Stumps of different sizes call for different removal approaches, says Sara Gottlieb, founder and CEO of Liminal Gardens.

“Start by measuring the diameter of the flat, cut surface at its widest point, while accounting for any large bulges or irregular shapes,” says Gottlieb. “You’ll also want to consider the ground-level root flare, surface roots, and the height of the stump above the ground. Together, these measurements help give you a better sense of the stump’s overall size. A stump under 12 inches in diameter would generally be considered small, while one measuring more than 30 inches would be considered large. Surface roots and stump height should also factor into your assessment.”

Small stumps can be ground out in a matter of minutes, whereas massive stumps may be too big for practical grinding. Chemical or fire stump removal can cause enough damage to large stumps that they are indeed “killed” and might not need full removal; the roots will stop growing if the stump is effectively killed off. For medium-sized stumps, it’s more a matter of your budget, patience, and DIY know-how when it comes to which method you choose from the options below.

Almost every expert we reached out to for tree-stump removal tips recommended using a chemical herbicide to quickly and effectively vanquish unwanted tree stumps. For many of our pros, it was the top suggestion. Benjamin Hanley of Hanley Landscape Design tells AD that “targeted herbicides like glyphosate (potassium nitrate) or triclopyr can be applied directly to a fresh cut or in drilled holes in the stump to kill the root system.” This can be a highly effective way to completely kill off a stump, but be warned: Those chemicals can be dangerous. It’s crucial to use proper protection—and to keep kids and pets at bay—if you’re using this tree-stump removal method.

· Herbicide (potassium nitrate or triclopyr)

Herbicide has been applied into the drilled holes of this tree stump.

Use a chainsaw to cut the stump down as short as you safely can. Next, drill multiple holes down into the stump, with the goal of sinking them at least eight to 10 inches down.

Generously pour your herbicide of choice down into each of the holes you drilled, taking extra care not to get any of the powder or liquid on exposed skin or anywhere near your face. Then pour about a cup of water into each hole to activate the chemicals.

Cover the treated tree stump with a tarp. Secure the tarp with bungees, ropes, rocks, or a combination of items heavy enough to keep it down tightly. Within a matter of days, that stump should be effectively dead, but the process may stretch out a bit depending on the stump’s resilience. (See below FAQ on how long it takes to kill a tree stump.)

“The tarp keeps rain out and helps retain heat and moisture, speeding up decomposition,” says Gabe Boersma of Top It or Drop It Tree Service. He advises checking on the treated stump every few weeks, and “within a few months, the stump should be soft enough to break apart with an axe or shovel.”

For smaller tree stumps, you may be able to simply rip the stump and its root system out of the ground using a shovel, a pick, and some elbow grease. (Ask me about the seven or eight hours I spent battling the root structure of a rather small Japanese maple tree in the summer of 2017.) For larger stumps, “our preferred method of removal is to grind the stump,” says Hanley. “A grinder can be used to remove it below grade with minimal site disturbance. We often grind the root system as well. Homeowners can rent a compact stump grinder from a store like Home Depot or Lowe’s, or call your local tree company to grind it.”

Be warned that a stump grinder can be a serious expense. “Renting [a stump grinder] typically costs between $300 and $500, while purchasing one outright can cost approximately $1,500 to $2,000,” says Gottlieb. Before choosing the stump-grinding approach, she advises you to make sure you have adequate access to and space around the stump for the grinding equipment. “Different types of grinders are suited to different stump sizes, and you’ll need enough room to maneuver the machine, along with an electrical hookup to power it.”

Whether you rent or buy a stump grinder or hire professionals to come in and use one for you, this is the most expensive way to remove a tree stump. But it might be worth the money: Stump grinding is by far and away the fastest approach; it can be the most effective, as well.

If you have a chainsaw and feel safe using it, cut the stump as low to the ground as you can. Then clear away as much debris as possible, as the chainsawing process will almost certainly kick up sawdust, fallen twigs, leaves, and loose rocks. Do not let your chainsaw hit the ground! Dirt not only dulls the chain instantly, but it can also cause dangerous kickback, send rocks and other debris flying, and generally be very, very bad. In fact, if there is visible dirt on any part of the stump you’ll be cutting, including roots, rinse off thoroughly with water, then let the stump dry fully before any sawing.

Set the stump grinder in place with its cutting wheel over the stump, then fire it up and slowly lower it down. Once the cutting wheel begins to make contact with the stump, move it from side to side and forward and back as needed to slowly grind away the tree stump.

Use the stump grinder to sever and grind large tree roots you see exposed in the grind-down process; when you’re done grinding both the stump and the root system, be sure to fill the hole you have created with soil, packing it until it’s leveled off. Consider using the ground stump bits as mulch.

It’s important to address the whole root system when killing a tree stump.

If you plan to use fire to kill a tree stump, please, put safety first, second, and third! Make sure there are no overhanging limbs that could combust; cut back and remove nearby grasses, brambles, and underbrush; and have a fire extinguisher ready to deal with any embers that float away.

Despite the many hazards one must be aware of before choosing this tree-stump removal method, there are good arguments to be made for using fire to eliminate your tree stump. “The burning method deserves special attention because it does not require uprooting the stump by hand or using heavy equipment, which can be a challenge if the stump is in a hard-to-reach area,” says Josh Heston, co-owner of ALC Property Maintenance. “The process does not take much time but does require attention to safety.”

Ideally you would do this using a doorknob drill bit or one similar to it, making a large hole in the center of the stump and drilling down as far as you can. Then, with a smaller bit (think a half-inch), drill into the sides of the stump until you reach the main hole. (Take note: This approach will not work with extra-wide stumps, though you may be able to use it by drilling a series of holes down into the top of the stump and connecting to each hole from the side. It’s a process, to be sure, but this approach can be very effective and may be worth trying even for larger tree stumps.)

Taking great care (and wearing gloves), soak the strip or strips of cotton in gas or lighter fluid, then insert all but a few inches of the fabric into the center hole. Switch gloves for safety (be aware of gasoline residue) and then light the fabric. Make sure you are leaning well back from the hole as you apply flame, and remember to wear protective eyewear during this stage; no need for you to end up as a comical internet meme without eyebrows as a result of this process.

“In order for the stump to start burning from the inside, you need to provide an oxygen supply,” says Heston. “For this, periodically blow air through the side holes. Also, from time to time, toss in some dry branches into the central hole to maintain the flame inside.” And do not squirt in gas or lighter fluid; that’s riskier than it’s worth.

It may take several hours for a stump to burn up enough that it can be removed easily with shovels and picks. Even if you don’t plan to fully remove the stump—you just needed to kill it—the burning technique will work and is relatively low-impact.

You don’t need to use fire, harsh chemicals, or heavy machinery to kill a tree stump; you can opt for a much more “natural” approach—but it will take time. Essentially, for the “natural method,” per Boersma, you’ll use “the same equipment as with the chemical [approach], but swap out chemicals for epsom salt or rock salt.”

Epsom salt or rock salt can be used to kill a tree stump.

If you have one, use a chainsaw and cut the stump as low as you safely can. (Again take heed of the notes above on chainsaw stump-removal safety, avoiding the blade from touching dirt or rocks and so on.) Then, drill several wide holes into the stump.

Pour in enough rock or epsom salt to fill each hole you drilled, then pour over enough water to fully saturate the salt. If the salt seems to all wash down into the hole, repeat the process one or two more times, adding more salt, then more water. If a stump is particularly porous (rotting, for example) then you may need to add salt and water two or more times.

Wrap the stump in a durable tarp and secure it in place. Then it’s time to play the waiting game. “This process is slow, taking 6 to 12 months, but is nontoxic and requires very little labor,” says Michael Clarke, the founder of Yardwork. Eventually, the stump will be so broken down that the ground will reclaim it or you can remove it with a shovel.

Our experts stressed the need for caution around chemicals, fire, chainsaws, and the heavy machinery (like stump grinders) one might make use of to kill a tree stump, but safe stump removal also involves really knowing what’s going on under the ground, says Sal Bracale, president of Moon Valley Nurseries. “Always call utility companies before you dig; this is the best advice I would give. Safety is always a concern, so wear proper PPE [personal protective equipment].”

And don’t ever use a brute-force approach to tree-stump removal, Bracale says. “[Killing a tree stump] is a lot of work and effort, but using unsafe techniques like a truck and a chain can cause serious injury if the chain comes off and backlashes toward a home or the truck.” You may well damage or ruin your vehicle. When in doubt, Bracale adds, “Hire a professional who is educated, experienced, licensed, and insured.”

The most common household products you can use to kill tree stumps include epsom salts and rock salts, as noted above, but there are other things you likely have around the house that can be used as well. Like the salts (and stronger herbicidal chemicals), both of the following products should be applied by pouring them down holes you drill into the stump.

You can use undiluted bleach (be careful not to breathe in the fumes) or white vinegar, and make sure to wrap the stump tightly in an airtight tarp after pouring in either of the DIY stump killer fluid. Do not—repeat—do not ever use bleach and vinegar at the same time for anything. Ever. Mixing these two substances can create a dangerous and even deadly gas.

While it could be considered the most labor-intensive and costliest way to fully destroy and remove a tree stump, grinding the stump is the fastest method of removal by far. You can remove a tree stump via grinding in an hour or two, as opposed to the weeks or months it can take to kill off then dig up a stump with chemicals or other products. “Especially for large stumps that need to be removed quickly, it’s best to use a stump grinder,” says Clarke. Larger stumps may resist salts or chemicals, and may continue to resprout new shoots or harbor pests and fungi for a long while.

With a stump grinder, you can kill a tree stump in an hour or two, give or take the preparation and cleanup time. On the far extreme, David Brown, owner of Reliable Tree Service, notes that it can take “six months to two years” to kill off a tree stump via “natural decomposition, [which is] the best approach for eco-conscious or low-budget approaches if you have the time to wait.”

The stump itself won’t damage buried water lines, per se, but the roots can be ruthless with pipes. Emily Demirdonder, cofounder and director of operations and marketing at Proximity Plumbing, says, “Homeowners usually focus on what’s sitting aboveground, but the real risk is what the roots are doing underneath.”

Tree (or stump) roots can spread two to three times the width of the tree’s canopy underground; they grow toward water and nutrients, and clay or PVC pipes are a direct source of both. “Drainage lines are essentially a target,” Demirdonder says. “The stump isn’t safe just because the tree is gone; live roots keep growing for months after removal, and in my work, I’ve tracked root systems traveling over four meters from the original stump during drain repairs. The tree above is dead, but the root network below is still very much active.... I believe if the stump sits within three meters of a drain line, full removal is the right call. Leaving it creates a slow root-intrusion problem that rarely shows surface signs until it’s already serious. The roots infiltrate through tiny joints or cracks, expand from inside, and the pipe collapses gradually. You won’t see it coming until there’s a slow drain or a wet patch in the yard, and by then the damage is usually well underway.”

The most basic reason to kill off a tree stump is to reclaim the space; maybe it’s in the middle of your backyard and the kids want to play there, or it would make for less hassle for you and your lawn mower. Maybe it’s in the middle of your garden and you want more planting space. The list could go on.

But there are other valid reasons that you may want to kill a tree stump—reasons that can protect your home and can protect other trees and plants nearby. “Fungal decay [from a stump] can spread to nearby plants, and the rotting wood often attracts pests,” says Hanley. Adding to that, Boersma explains that “dead stumps can attract pests like termites, carpenter ants, or fungi that can spread to nearby healthy trees or even your home’s structure.”

Yes, a tree can sometimes grow back from a stump, but it depends mainly on the species of the tree and the condition of the roots left behind. When a tree is cut down and its root system remains alive, some species are able to send up new shoots from the stump itself or from the roots, in a natural process called coppicing. Tree species such as oak, willow, maple, poplar, birch, and eucalyptus are especially good at this and can regrow surprisingly quickly, particularly if the tree was relatively young and healthy when it was cut down. On the other hand, most conifers (evergreens like pine, spruce, fir, and cedar) generally do not regrow from stumps because they lack the ability to produce new shoots from old wood, so once they are cut down, the stumps typically die. Other factors also influence whether regrowth happens, including the age of the tree (again, younger trees respond better and tend to grow back), the overall health of the root system, how high the stump was cut, and even the season in which the tree was removed.

As long as that tree stump isn’t putting buried pipes at risk, or acting as a hotbed for pests (and isn’t going to be a pain to mow around), it might be best left right where it is—and that’s true even if it’s rather prominent on your property.

“Removal isn’t the only option; a tree stump can also become part of your landscape design,” says Gottlieb. “Building up a mound of plantings around it offers a way to incorporate the stump into the garden and build on previous iterations of the landscape. The stump itself can serve as a bench, or it can be carved to create an artistic focal point. Leaving it in place can also reduce the disruption to the property that full root removal would cause. Planting around and on the stump, working into the crevices between surface roots, and layering moss and flowering perennials can add depth and visual interest to the garden.”

#4994. BTC heads into US midterm showdown: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week

Bitcoin price action held its 100-day moving average into the monthly close as crypto markets braced for US midterm election and tech earnings volatility.

Bitcoin (BTC) held above its 100-day moving average on Monday ahead of US midterm elections, jobs data and earnings from Apple and Palantir.

Tuesday’s US midterm elections will determine control of Congress, with prediction market traders heavily favoring a Democratic victory in the House of Representatives.

Kalshi put the probability of Democrats winning the House at 93.6% as of Monday.

President Donald Trump said he would use his veto power if Democrats took control of Congress.

“I guess I’ll become Mr Veto. They’ll be sending stuff up. You veto it,” he said, according to the New York Post.

US midterm elections odds (screenshot). Source: Kalshi

Bitcoin ended the fourth quarter lower in each of the past three US midterm election years, falling 17.3% in 2014, 43.5% in 2018 and 14.8% in 2022. All three periods coincided with Bitcoin bear markets.

Benjamin Cowen, founder and CEO of crypto analytics platform IntoTheCryptoverse, suggested that the midterms can function as a cue to increase BTC exposure due to their short-term bearish impact on price.

“Usually the Q4 dump of midterm years just provide opportunities to buy for those who sold long ago,” he said Friday on X.

In July, Cowen referenced Bitcoin bear-market bottoms coinciding with the second half of midterm years.

BTC/USD was down 6.4% for the quarter as of Monday, after its weakest October since 2014, according to CoinGlass.

BTC/USD liquidation heatmap. Source: CoinGlass

September US job openings data are due Tuesday, followed by October’s nonfarm payrolls report on Friday.

Payrolls are expected to rise by 65,000, after the economy added 29,000 jobs in September, below forecasts for 84,000. Such an outcome notionally increases the odds of dovish policy signals from the Federal Reserve, which is in turn bullish for crypto and risk-asset liquidity.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Fed Governor Michelle Bowman are among the officials due to speak this week.

Data from CME Group’s FedWatch Tool currently shows that markets expect the Fed to raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points at the December meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The odds of such an outcome have sat between 67% and 75% for the past month.

Fed target rate probability comparison for December FOMC meeting (screenshot). Source: CME Group

The University of Michigan will also release its preliminary November consumer sentiment survey on Friday, including consumers’ inflation expectations.

Alongside the macro data prints, 20% of S&P 500 companies are due to report earnings in the coming days. Chief among these are tech giants Apple and Palantir, both due to report after the market close on Monday.

The reports follow last week’s tech sell-off, when disappointing guidance renewed concerns about AI spending and profitability.

Economist Mohamed El-Erian described markets as now “acutely sensitive” to tech-sector news headlines in weekend analysis.

“The market is particularly focused on justification for the massive capital expenditures being deployed across the sector, ROI’s, and revenue growth,” he wrote.

After closing October down 7.3%, Bitcoin is holding above a moving average that has provided support since mid-August.

Related: Here’s what happened in crypto today

TradingView data showed BTC/USD staying above last week’s low near $76,300, without retesting it around the monthly close.

That low was close to the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) for BTC/USD, which has since risen to $76,548.

Bitcoin also reclaimed its 100-week exponential moving average (EMA) in time for the monthly close, with this standing at $77,759.

BTC/USD daily chart with 100 SMA, 100 EMA. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Trader and analyst Rekt Capital compared the weekly chart with Bitcoin’s rebound from its 2022 bear market low. During the recovery, BTC/USD produced an inverse head-and-shoulders pattern, retested support at the right shoulder, briefly fell below it and then rallied.

Last week’s drop to $76,300 brought Bitcoin back to what Rekt Capital identified as right-shoulder support on the current chart. He is watching for a brief move below that level as a possible next step in the comparison.

“The question now is whether Bitcoin can produce some sort of downside deviation below here over the next few weeks,” Rekt Capital said.

BTC/USD one-week chart. Source: Rekt Capital on X.com

#4991. How T7X Is Building the Infrastructure for a New Era of Capital Markets

How T7X Is Building the Infrastructure for a New Era of Capital Markets

Most tokenized stocks aren't natively issued on a blockchain. They begin as conventional shares, sit with a broker or custodian, and are then represented by tokens issued separately. In effect, the market has largely replicated traditional securities structures on-chain instead of rethinking them from the ground up. The token "may track the value of the underlying shares," writes Ivan Kan, CMO of tokenization platform T7X, in an essay shared with Decrypt, "but the token holder is not necessarily the shareholder of record."

While the holder owns the price movement, whether they own the share is another matter altogether. The SEC set out three models in January: issuers tokenizing their own shares, third parties issuing tokens against shares held in custody, and firms issuing a separate security for synthetic exposure.

Writing for Forbes' Technology Council in August, Kan cited Pantera Capital research covering 593 tokenized assets across 11 asset classes, of which 77.6% were what Pantera called "digital wrappers around traditional infrastructure" rather than securities in their own right.

"What does the token legally represent, and who authorized it?" Kan asks, setting out an alternative model that T7X Equities is pursuing, which they dub "native issuance." A security exists because an issuer authorizes it, they argue, and "blockchain does not eliminate those corporate and securities-law requirements."

Under the native issuance model, the token is part of the authorized issuance from the start, running from issuer authorization to investor verification to transfer-agent validation, aiming at "one security, one authorized issuance, one ownership record, one digital representation."

Wyoming, Delaware, and Nevada corporate law recognizes a "certificate token," allowing shares to be represented electronically on a blockchain. T7X is incorporated in Wyoming and structures its issuances to operate within this framework. The blockchain then becomes "part of the infrastructure supporting the capitalization table" instead of being just another instrument layered on top.

The transfer agent keeps the official master securityholder file and the blockchain records transactions, while the legal record of ownership stays where regulators expect it.

In T7X's administrated offerings, that transfer agent is T7X Equities. Transfer agents register with the SEC and hold the authoritative record of who owns a security, processing transfers and maintaining the master file, which puts the company inside the model it is advocating as well as behind it. Its first example is Tranquil Healthcare Fund I, a Tier 2 Regulation A+ offering of up to $75 million that the SEC qualified on June 29. T7X Equities issues tokens representing its shares on Trusted Smart Chain and delivers them to investors' wallets, the company said.

"There's a registered, SEC-regulated gatekeeper that determines who owns which security at any point in time," T7X Chief Executive Pablo Penaloza said at Consensus in Miami earlier this year. "As long as you have a transfer agent involved, there is no way that securities can disappear without trace."

Kan calls the broader category "RWA+." The plus doesn't refer to any single rule, he argues, but the requirement that "compliance and oversight are real," and it rests on three elements. Native issuance creates the token as part of the security's authorized issuance. Integrated compliance writes investor verification and disclosure into the instrument from the start, not as an afterthought. Legally enforceable ownership puts the token holder on the transfer agent's record.

"A receipt is not an asset," Kan wrote in Forbes. "It is a claim wrapped around one, dependent on an intermediary to honor it." Synthetic "PreStocks" tied to SpaceX and Anthropic were never valid claims, he noted, because neither company authorized the transfers. Done properly, he argues, "ownership, compliance and settlement are the same fact."

Whether a token carries the rights of a share is becoming the dividing line elsewhere, too. The SEC's new innovation exemption covers tokenized stocks carrying dividends and voting rights while excluding price-tracking synthetics, and Nasdaq's arrangement with Kraken turns on tokens conveying the same voting rights as ordinary shares.

Penaloza pins the near-term opportunity on companies raising under $100 million, usually between $50 million and $75 million, through Regulation A offerings.

Regulation A+, Kan argues, suits this model because it permits public solicitation and non-accredited participation while requiring audited financials and continuing disclosure. Most tokenized assets rely instead on Regulation D placements, limited to accredited investors. Reg A also opens the door, Penaloza notes, to retirement accounts. Unregistered securities can legally sit in a self-directed IRA, but many brokers won't hold them and most investment advisers steer clients away. "The money is sitting in the older generations' retirement accounts," he said, and a registration attached to the investment is what makes an individual retiree comfortable holding it.

For investors already holding these securities, the benefit is an exit. Shareholders in Reg A and Reg D placements typically receive a paper certificate and then "have to go around and find somebody who will want to give them liquidity," Penaloza said. A native digital security can trade on a secondary market, he said, settling wallet to wallet without a custodian in between.

Giving Reg A and Reg D holdings somewhere to trade would, he argued, "incredibly speed up not only the rate of capital formation, but also the liquidity in the market." Within five years, he predicts, "the total tokenized portfolio will far surpass the existing market capitalization of what is currently trading on all the public markets."

To find out more about T7X’s real-world asset tokenization platform, head to t7x.com.

#4989. Where Does Christine Baranski Live? Exploring the Gilded Age Star’s Real Estate Portfolio

Her Gilded Age character lives in a grand Upper East Side brownstone, but where does Christine Baranski live? The Emmy- and Tony–winning actor was born in Buffalo, New York, and still owns property in her home state in the form of a Manhattan pied-à-terre—and yes, like Agnes van Rhijn’s onscreen dwelling, it is on the Upper East Side. However, the Good Wife star primarily lives in Connecticut, where her late husband grew up and where the couple raised their two daughters, Isabel and Lily.

Read on to learn more about Baranski’s property portfolio.

For decades, Baranski has lived in Connecticut’s Litchfield County. Her first visit to the region was on a 1982 motorcycle ride; her future husband, fellow actor Matthew Cowles, was the driver. Cowles grew up in an 18th-century farmhouse in the small town of Bethlehem. “I had such a feeling of destiny about it,” Baranski recalled in a 2008 interview, “I loved it. I loved the smells in the air, the farms, the field. It was a dream. When Matthew took me into his home, I thought, ‘We’re gonna raise children here.’” The couple married the next year, briefly residing in an NYC apartment before returning to raise their daughters, born in 1984 and in 1987, in Cowles’s childhood home. “I had such a sense of eternity, like I was meant to be there,” she added.

A 2003 interview reported that Baranski primarily lived in Bethlehem and maintained a lake house about half an hour away, and it seems that this is still the case. “I have a marvelous house on a lake in Connecticut and I’ve hosted some very famous actors there,” the actor said in a recent interview with The Guardian, adding that those famed visitors have, on occasion, stripped naked for a swim. “It has a very long dock that has been ‘grandfathered’ in, as in they don’t allow a dock that long to be built anymore, but this is about 100 years old. You sit in the living room in summer and watch the sun set, and then go out into the evening and skinny dip in the lake.”

Cowles died in 2014, but Baranski remains deeply rooted in his hometown. The Mamma Mia! star is so entrenched in the community that she became active in the Housatonic Valley Association, a local environmental nonprofit, and currently serves as one of its directors. “I enjoy so much the beauty of Litchfield County,” Baranski said in 2009. “I couldn't imagine living in a more beautiful place.”

In 2004, Baranski bought a pied-à-terre on Manhattan’s Upper East Side for $1.27 million. Located in a 1920s structure where Jackie Kennedy lived as a child, the two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment featured a 21-foot-long living room with hardwood floors, a wood-burning fireplace flanked by built-in bookshelves, and yellow-striped wallpaper. A galley kitchen opened to a small dining room painted a soft sage green and decorated with elegant paintings in ornate gold frames, while the bedrooms were done up in distinct palettes: one was blue and white, while the other was tan with pops of red and orange. Both had their own en suite bath.

“Happily, now after years of commuting to LA and trying to do the whole bicoastal thing, The Good Wife shoots in Greenpoint, Brooklyn,” Baranski said in a 2011 New York Times article. “Our kids are grown up and in graduate school, so I have this life where I can enjoy the city and not worry about racing home to Connecticut.” The actor shared her typical Sunday routine in the city, which included reading in a café, visiting museums, and seeing friends. “I tend to call Sundays a girlfriend day because my husband is in Connecticut, so more often than not I’m alone here, which is a chance to catch up with girlfriends,” she said. “I might do a lunch at one of the hole-in-the-wall French bistros in the neighborhood, but sometimes I skip lunch in favor of an early dinner.” Then, the actor turns in early. “If I’m in town on a Sunday, it usually means I’m working Monday, and often I’m the first shot of the day, which means you’re up at 4:30. That means going to bed early. So I’ll go to my early dinner and then try to get myself to sleep by 9 or 9:30.”

Inhabitants of the co-op building, designed by architect Lafayette A. Goldstone, have access to a backyard garden, a gym, and a laundry room. Baranski listed her unit in the nine-story building in February 2021 for $1.39 million, and it sold that June.

Baranski didn’t move too far, however. In December 2020, the Good Fight star upgraded to a larger $2.2 million duplex unit in the same building. Listing photos showed that the home was sold with a few spaces under construction, so she likely added some custom touches before moving in. The apartment has four bedrooms, three bathrooms, and a much larger eat-in kitchen than the one found in Baranski’s previous unit. It still boasts a wood-burning fireplace in the living room, accessed from the foyer through an arched doorway. On its other end, the living room opens to a spacious formal dining room. A guest bedroom rounds out the lower level. The remaining bedrooms are at the top of a winding staircase. Another fireplace, tucked between built-ins, graces one bedroom, which shares a Jack-and-Jill bathroom with another bedroom—which could be used as a dressing room—that boasts six closets. The final bedroom has a full en suite bathroom.

#4988. Hong Kong takes tokenized settlement to 24/7, plans stablecoin trials

The HKMA plans to bring regulated stablecoins into tokenized government debt trials, while HSBC says its RedCoin stablecoin has reached 50,000 users.

Hong Kong has expanded its Project Ensemble pilot to allow round-the-clock settlement of tokenized transactions, as the city’s monetary regulator prepares to bring regulated stablecoins into trials involving tokenized government debt.

On Monday, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said that it had advanced its EnsembleTX project to a new stage allowing 24/7 real-value transactions. The HKMA said the update would help banks and their clients move funds globally, manage tokenized investments and handle treasury operations outside conventional settlement hours.

Participating banks initially settled payments through Hong Kong’s existing dollar settlement system, which limited settlement hours. When the pilot began real-value trials in November 2025, the HKMA said it planned to introduce tokenized central bank money to allow settlement around the clock.

The HKMA launched Project Ensemble in March 2024 to explore how banks could settle tokenized transactions using wholesale central bank digital money. A sandbox opened that August, allowing banks to connect their tokenized deposit platforms and test transactions.

Speaking at Hong Kong FinTech Week on Monday, HKMA Chief Executive Eddie Yue said the regulator was introducing tokenized central bank money as a “foundation layer” for 24/7 settlement. He said tokenized bonds, money market funds and bank deposits were already being used.

The HKMA also said recognized dealers had completed secondary-market trial trades in tokenized Exchange Fund Bills, a form of short-term debt issued by the regulator. It plans to expand those trials to include regulated stablecoins.

Separately, HSBC Group CEO Georges Elhedery said at Hong Kong FinTech Week that the bank’s recently launched Hong Kong dollar stablecoin, RedCoin, had reached 50,000 users about 10 days after its debut.

“We have 50,000 users,” Elhedery said, adding that HSBC was targeting “multi-million users” as it expands access to the token.

RedCoin’s rollout brings stablecoins to retail payments, while Ensemble’s settlement work has focused on transactions involving banks and tokenized investments.

Elhedery said HSBC was also offering tokenized deposits to wholesale clients in Hong Kong and about half a dozen other jurisdictions, allowing funds to move around the clock.

Related: Hong Kong prepares banks for quantum threats amid tokenization push

The bank launched RedCoin on Oct. 23 for transfers and merchant payments through its PayMe application. HSBC said more than 3.3 million PayMe customers could activate stablecoin wallets to use the token. It also plans to bring the stablecoin into its mobile banking app and allow subscriptions to tokenized investments, including a Hong Kong dollar money market fund share class.

HSBC was among Hong Kong’s first licensed stablecoin issuers in April alongside Anchorpoint Financial, a venture backed by Animoca Brands and Standard Chartered. The city’s licensing regime, introduced in August 2025, requires issuers to meet standards for backing reserves, redemption and risk management.

#4986. Bitmine Buys More Ethereum as Tom Lee Calls the Binance Hack Bullish

Bitmine Buys More Ethereum as Tom Lee Calls the Binance Hack Bullish

Bitmine Immersion Technologies kept its weekly Ethereum buying streak intact, adding 8,573 ETH worth roughly $19 million, while chairman Tom Lee used the record Binance hack to argue that crypto has grown more resilient, not more fragile.

The NYSE-listed company said Monday its holdings now total 6,060,506 ETH, worth roughly $13.7 billion at a reference price of $2,261 per coin.

That represents 4.9% of Ethereum’s 122.2 million token supply, leaving Bitmine, by its own count, 99% of the way to its goal of owning 5% of the network, a target it brands the “Alchemy of 5%,” reached in just 15 months. The firm has bought Ethereum every week since launching its treasury strategy on June 30, 2025.

Most of Lee’s commentary focused on last week’s roughly $6.4 billion theft from Binance, which the FBI has attributed to North Korea. Lee called it “a terrible development” but argued the market’s “relatively muted” reaction was “very constructive.” (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt’s parent company.)

Lee noted that when North Korea’s Lazarus-linked hackers drained $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025, Ethereum fell 8% that day and 20% within a week, whereas ETH slid just 4% after the Binance breach, despite the theft being roughly four times larger.

Lee laid out six reasons for the muted response: Binance’s ability to cover all customer losses, the absence of a cascade of DeFi failures like the one that followed Bybit, swift industry action that cut the potential loss in half, the FBI naming North Korea within two days rather than the months such attributions have taken historically, the fact that the exploit was a “corporate infiltration” of Binance’s infrastructure rather than a blockchain flaw, and the limited price downside itself, which he read as a sign a “crypto bull market is underway.”

Taken together, he said, the episode shows the industry is “increasingly resilient and more capable of absorbing these nation-state assaults.”

Counting cash, other tokens and what it calls “moonshot” investments, Bitmine’s total holdings stood at $14.5 billion as of Nov. 1, including 216 Bitcoin, $498 million in cash and marketable securities, a $180 million stake in Beast Industries and an $82 million position in Eightco Holdings, which it bills as a rare public proxy for indirect OpenAI exposure.

Bitmine remains the world’s largest Ethereum treasury and the second-largest crypto treasury overall, trailing only Michael Saylor’s Strategy, which the release said holds about 848,517 BTC.

Strategy recently resumed its own Bitcoin buying with a $66 million purchase after a brief pause.

Bitmine has 5,227,037 ETH, about 86% of its holdings, staked through its MAVAN platform, with projected annualized staking revenue of roughly $358 million.

#4985. What Is RED-S? Doctors Explain the Condition—and Why Women Are at Higher Risk

When it comes to exercise, there’s one thing that’s just as important as the training itself: fueling. Having the right nutrients—and enough calories—to sustain your activity and recover from it are critical for staying healthy, feeling your best, and keeping your body functioning in tip-top shape. After all, fueling your body isn't just about performing well today; it's about being able to keep doing what you love for years to come.

Eating can sometimes feel like an afterthought, especially when you’re busy with training, but consistently underfueling can actually result in a condition called relative energy deficiency in sport, or RED-S for short. And women have a much higher risk of developing RED-S compared to men. In a 2026 study in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, researchers found that 70 percent of high-level female athletes were at risk of developing RED-S.

Top-ranked tennis player Emma Navarro recently revealed that she is one of those athletes dealing with the condition. Earlier this month, she posted on Instagram, detailing her experience, which included extreme mood swings, brain fog, a weakened immune system, constant headaches, and bouts of dizziness. Exercises she could do with ease in the past suddenly felt impossible. She was also hungry, all the time. “I had been under-fueling for almost three years,” she wrote. “My body was fighting back any way it knew how.”

But, you don’t need to be an elite-level tennis player to experience the condition. Here’s what you need to know about RED-S, including how to spot—and stop—it early, according to experts.

Meet the experts: Elizabeth Matzkin, MD, is an orthopedic surgeon and chief of women’s sports medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Amy West, MD, is a sports medicine physician at Northwell Orthopedic Institute. Amy Stephens, RD, is a sports dietitian who specializes in eating disorders.

There’s a simple explanation behind what causes RED-S: It occurs when someone is not eating enough to meet the demands of their training—or even their body’s basic physiologic needs, says Elizabeth Matzkin, MD, an orthopedic surgeon and chief of women’s sports medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Your body needs energy not only to sustain you, say, on a run or in a weightlifting session, but it also needs energy to support bone health, hormone production, metabolism, immune function, and cardiovascular health.

When you’re consistently not consuming enough food to support your activity levels, over time, your body won’t have the energy it needs to support those critical functions, leading to a wide range of symptoms that define RED-S—which is more than medical jargon for undereating. It reflects what happens when your body is chronically underfueled and can lead to long-term health issues.

Anyone, from the elite athlete to someone training for their first half-marathon to the person increasing their lifting sessions in the gym while trying to lose weight, can be at risk of developing RED-S. Remember, the “r” in RED-S stands for relative; so it’s all about not meeting your energy needs, whatever they are.

When underfueling, in the short term, you may experience fatigue, impaired concentration, more frequent illnesses, poor recovery, and irregular periods or none at all, Dr. Matzkin says. When it comes to your sport, training and performance may suffer too. Low energy availability can make it harder to sustain a workout, decrease strength and endurance, or lead to muscle weakness or pain, says Amy West, MD, a sports medicine physician at Northwell Orthopedic Institute.

You’ll also be much more susceptible to injuries, particularly when it comes to your bones. This has impacts on the long term: “Adolescence and young adulthood are critical years for building peak bone mass, so prolonged low energy availability during this period may have consequences later in life,” Dr. Matzkin says. Down the line, that could mean osteoporosis. Meanwhile, missing your period for long periods of time can have impacts on future fertility, Dr. West adds.

Early stages of RED-S can happen pretty quickly, says Amy Stephens, RD, a sports dietitian who specializes in eating disorders. After just one day of underfueling, you’ll feel symptoms of “hanger”; after just a week, your body may stop building muscle and endurance. Then, she says, it could take six to nine months to fully recover.

RED-S is much more associated with women and girls compared to boys and men. Until 2014, RED-S was referred to as the “female athlete triad,” which highlighted the relationship between undereating, menstrual dysfunction, and decreased bone mineral density. While RED-S can happen to anyone, “female athletes are more vulnerable, especially in sports that emphasize leanness, endurance, aesthetics, or weight categories,” Dr. Matzkin says. (Think: Running, gymnastics, and diving.)

But, that’s not the only reason women may deal with RED-S more than men. There’s also the pressures that women face disproportionately to be thin, says Dr. West, and the fact that women are more likely to have eating disorders.

RED-S doesn’t happen all at once. Earlier, more subtle signs like fatigue and trouble sleeping pop up when a person has what docs call low energy availability, which occurs when they’re not eating enough to support their activity levels. As someone is continuously in a state of low energy availability, RED-S can occur.

Low energy availability and RED-S can affect almost every system in the body, but these are the areas you may most often see symptoms, according to the doctors.

If RED-S is suddenly on your radar now, don’t worry. You don’t need to completely overhaul your life or your training to avoid it. In fact, there are a few intuitive steps you can take to give yourself a good shot at fueling fully—no calorie tracking necessary. Here’s what you can do.

It’s so simple, but occasionally taking stock of how you’re feeling in and out of training can go a long way. The symptoms above are warning signs of not eating enough, but you should also know what a fully-fueled athlete feels like too. A well-fueled athlete has consistent energy all day, mostly only feels hungry around mealtimes, and doesn’t deal with brain fog, Stephens says. Their mood is stable, they recover well between workouts, and they sleep well too. It’s a good idea to check in and reflect on how you’ve been feeling lately—strong and energized and able to “kick” at the end of a workout, or sluggish and hungry, struggling to get in those last few reps.

Plus, if you wanted to dig even deeper, you can also get some more information from an annual blood workup with your doctor. Since RED-S affects so many systems in the body, Stephens says, you might see issues pop up across a range of tests, including your thyroid, white blood cell count, ferritin and iron, vitamin D, or complete blood count. If any of those are out of range, it could be due to underfueling, but they would need to be discussed with your doctor in the context of the rest of your health history and any other testing.

You don’t need to download a macro-tracking app or suddenly start counting calories to avoid RED-S. (For the record: Stephens doesn’t have her athletes do that.) Instead, focus simply on getting three meals per day, with your plate being about one-third protein, one-third carbs, and one-third vegetables each time. Most people don’t eat breakfast, Stephens says, and that’s often one of the quickest culprits when it comes to not having enough food in a day.

This is another simple reminder, but if you’re someone with a training plan on the horizon, keep in mind that what you’re eating now is not what you’ll be eating in the future, Stephens says. As plans progress and get more and more intense (you’re running longer distances or lifting heavier in the gym or simply adding another day of Solidcore per week), you’ll need to increase the amount of food you eat.

One helpful rule of thumb is that for every hour you spend working out, you should add on an extra 500 to 600 calories to your day, whether that’s with the help of snacks or larger serving sizes at meals, Stephens says. Then, anything in the 2-to-3-hour range will require in-session fueling, like gels on a long run.

If you’re noticing any of the above symptoms or suspect that you’re not fueling right, it’s a good idea to see a professional. Earlier signs like fatigue and poor sleep are easy to write off, but checking in and making sure they’re not a result of underfueling can keep low energy availability from developing into a full-on case of RED-S. In addition to setting an appointment with a doc, you can also try increasing your food intake by incorporating more snacks throughout your day or having larger portion sizes at meals. If you’re not already having a carb-rich snack before a workout, try adding that for some extra energy, paired with something high in protein and carbs afterward to support recovery.

Just keep in mind: It’s never too early to bring this up with a doctor or dietitian, whether you want help determining the appropriate calorie and macro goals for your workout demands or for them to evaluate symptoms you’re not so sure about. “Earlier evaluation is better,” Dr. Matzkin says. “We don't want to wait for a stress fracture—this means bone health has already been affected.” Ideally, you’ll talk with a doctor before reaching this point, but two symptoms that should send you to their office ASAP are frequent injuries, especially if you’re having a tough time recovering from them, and period irregularities, Dr. West says.

From there, treating RED-S is all about getting your body back to the right balance of energy intake to energy output and managing any injuries that may have arisen. You’ll likely need to work with a doctor and/or dietitian to help you get enough calories and nutrients and reduce your training demands while you get caught up. In addition to a sports medicine doc and/or dietitian, you may also work with a bone endocrine specialist (if your bone health has been affected) and/or a sports psychologist, Dr. Matzkin says.

Whether you are at risk for RED-S or not, consider this your reminder that fueling is critical for any active person. Being thoughtful about getting enough calories, carbs, and fat for energy, and protein for recovery is your best line of defense against the condition. While everyone’s needs will be different, a rule of thumb, per Dr. West: “Athletes often need more food than they think.”

Olivia Luppino is an associate editor at Women’s Health. She reports, writes, and edits content ranging from service stories to in-depth features and awards packages across all verticals, including health, fitness, sports, and beauty. While at WH, she’s traveled to Paris, France to watch Faith Kipyegon attempt a sub-4-minute mile and covered major races like Ultra Trail du Mont Blanc in Chamonix. Olivia is a RRCA-certified running coach who is especially passionate about helping people start their running journey and is training for her second marathon. Her works also appears in New York Magazine’s The Cut, PS (formerly Popsugar), and Salon, where she also did on-camera interviews with celebrity guests.

#4982. Brazil's Largest Exchange Mercado Bitcoin Halts Withdrawals After $40 Million Hack

Brazil's Largest Exchange Mercado Bitcoin Halts Withdrawals After $40 Million Hack

Brazil's largest crypto exchange, Mercado Bitcoin, suspended deposits and withdrawals on Monday after identifying a security incident in one of its systems in the early hours of the morning. The exchange said no customer lost money and no data leaked.

"We identified and quickly contained a security incident in one of our systems early this morning," Mercado Bitcoin said in a Portuguese-language statement on X. "As a preventive protection measure, deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended."

Blockchain security firm Hypernative flagged more than $40 million in suspicious transfers that may be linked to the incident, according to a preliminary analysis that spans at least 10 blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and Tron. Mercado Bitcoin has not confirmed that figure and has not disclosed how the attackers got in.

In a follow-up post, the exchange published the destination addresses it identified on five networks: EVM chains (blockchains built to run the same code as Ethereum), Bitcoin, Solana, Stellar, and Tron. It said the addresses were released only so others can identify and track the funds on-chain.

Identificamos e contivemos com rapidez um incidente de segurança em um de nossos sistemas nesta madrugada.

Reforçamos que:• Não houve nenhum prejuízo aos clientes;• Não houve vazamento de dados.

Como medida preventiva de proteção, depósitos e saques…

— Mercado Bitcoin (@MercadoBitcoin) November 2, 2026

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said in a post on X that the stablecoin issuer has frozen more than 4.5 million USDT connected to the incident.

USDT is a dollar-pegged stablecoin, and Tether can blacklist the addresses holding it so the tokens cannot be moved, though a freeze does not by itself return the funds to their owner.

Tether froze more than 4.5M USDT related to this security incident. https://t.co/PCtP4957jn

— Paolo Ardoino 🤖 (@paoloardoino) November 2, 2026

The incident comes days after hackers drained more than $6 billion from Binance on October 29, a theft the FBI attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has since reopened withdrawals and said it replenished about 95% of the affected assets. Mercado Bitcoin has not linked the two incidents and has not said who is behind its own.

Deposits and withdrawals at Mercado Bitcoin remain suspended, and the exchange has not given a date for resuming them. It said it will post regular updates on X.

#4981. Women’s Heart Health Just Got a Major Update. Here’s What Doctors Want You to Know

This is a much-needed and overdue change.

Big news in female heart health: Four major health organizations have come together to create a shared framework and clinical guidance for women's heart health across several different life stages.

The American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine came together to outline the “female life stage" framework to protect heart health from puberty through menopause and beyond. The framework (which essentially acts as a classification system for medical providers) was just published in the journal Circulation.

This is a big deal for many reasons, including acknowledging that female heart health and risk factors change over a woman's life. "This has been a long time coming," says Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California.

According to the American Heart Association, cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in women, claiming more lives than breast cancer, lung cancer, and chronic lung disease combined. But only four in 10 women are aware that cardiovascular disease is the biggest threat to their health.

This new framework separates cardiovascular risk factors, along with care needs, throughout the different stages of a woman's life. Here's what you need to know.

Meet the experts: Sadiya Khan, MD, chair of the collaborative writing group and professor of Cardiovascular Epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine; Jennifer Haythe, MD, co-director of the Women’s Heart Center at NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center; and Nicole Weinberg, MD, cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California

The Female Life Stage framework is defined by hormone changes specific to girls and women at different stages of life, hence the name. The framework also recognizes pregnancy as an event that can impact cardiovascular health at any or several life stages. Here's a breakdown of each:

Adopting this new way of classifying female life stages “offers a transformative opportunity to equitably improve cardiovascular health for all girls and women," the researchers wrote in the review article.

This has never been done before. “For the first time, four major medical groups agree that a woman’s heart health is shaped by every stage of her life, from her first period to menopause," says Jennifer Haythe, MD, co-director of the Women’s Heart Center at NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

This helps address the "fragmentation of care" that can happen between ob-gyns, cardiologists, and other specialists who care for women, says Sadiya Khan, MD, chair of the collaborative writing group and professor of Cardiovascular Epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. "We're all speaking different languages and we're all speaking different levels of care, yet they're all connected," she says.

The framework is a "shared playbook" that doctors from different specialties can use to guide patient care, along with a language that's understandable and easy to communicate for everyone, Dr. Khan says. "It's really connecting those aspects of health that we think are disconnected," she says.

This new system helps to bridge the gap between viewing cardiovascular care as something completely separate from women's health. "This is meant to reframe cardiovascular health as part of a woman's care," says Dr. Khan. "Any of these things may influence the other."

Weinberg says the framework will create "a more unified view" of women's health. "By creating a road map that is shared by pediatricians, cardiologists, ob-gyns, and maternal-fetal medicine doctors, things like PMOS, irregular periods, pregnancy complications, and metabolic shifts in perimenopause will be treated as real heart health signals, so early warning signs aren’t missed," Haythe says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.
