#4979. 10 Best Bedside Lamps & Table Lamps (2026)

Before you spin into a redecorating frenzy (step away from the chandeliers…), consider the transformative power of the table lamp. The best bedside lamps are a necessary lighting addition to any bedroom—nighttime reader or not. They also have staying power away from the bedside, should they find their home in another part of the house as your taste shifts: add them to a shelf on a bookcase, show them off in an entryway, let one adorn your kitchen countertop.

Accent lighting has always been a thing, but lately, with the rise of anti–Big Light content on TikTok and Reels, the demand for cute, trendy ambient lighting options is going way up. And we get it—relying on built-in overhead light fixtures feels cold and corporate, while smaller lamps create a warmer ambience. That’s why we had the bright idea to test a curated selection of top picks from some of our favorite brands (in addition to other great options that score high design marks in our books). In each of our reviews you’ll find an AD editor’s testimony as to what makes each light stand out, how they use it in their space, and what’s something buyers should keep in mind. The hardest part now will be deciding on just one (or two).

(Lamps pictured with a 2.4-ounce candle for size comparison)

The head is magnetized, so you can direct light in pretty much any direction you choose.

Flos’s Bilboquet Table Lamp, designed by Philippe Malouin, is another seen-before decor moment, as we tapped it for our 2025 gifting shoot. It’s been a mainstay at Fletcher’s work station ever since. “This sexy little lamp has a great glow and looks just as handsome when it isn't turned on,” she told us. “I keep it at my desk and it's a lovely distraction from the standard issue fluorescents here at 1WTC. I love that the bulbous chrome joint is a functional swivel point, which means it can spotlight almost 360 degrees.” An eco-friendly design as well, Flos crafted the lamp’s body from a byproduct of paper production and refrained from using any glue, so the components will be recyclable after a long life spent spotlighting your home.

A built-in dimmer switch allows you to customize the glow.

The switch requires a substantial turn to activate and may not be the best choice for illuminating a full workspace. If the Raffia Wave shade isn’t your style, there’s three other shade options available, along with a range of colored bases.

Looking for some living room table lighting with a touch of coastal grandma style? Look no further than this rattan lamp from Serena and Lily. With its petite size, the light can fill up empty nooks and crannies while perfectly illuminating them. “What immediately caught my eye was how the unique, trendy raffia shade complements the sleek ceramic base beautifully,” associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz told us. “The lamp is the perfect size for a desk or kitchen counter, adding a warm, ambient glow and delightful pop of style.”

A button controls this lamp's four-step dimmer.

If you're looking for a super bright desk or task lamp, this is not it! I'd also opt for a non matte option in the future because the black shows all the imperfections which, because I tote it around a lot, there are many bumps and bruises.

If you have an outdoor space, you know the importance of having a cordless lamp you can tote on the short journey inside to grab more drinks or snacks once the sun has gone down. Or maybe you want to guide guests to the backyard for a little midnight gossip session around the fire pit. Whatever it is, this rechargeable lamp is easy to grab and is available in a plethora of colors. With a “vaguely mushroomy” look according to Rachel, its small stature and four dimmable light levels makes it endlessly versatile. “I've seen them featured in Hypebeast homes, minimalist Barcelona bedrooms, tiny Sydney apartments, and grand Austin estates, so chances are it'll work for whatever design scheme resonates with you,” says Rachel. “The last note I'd make is that the price point is quite steep at over $300 for such a tiny piece. While there are lots of dupes on the market, I'd definitely stick with the original as it's been through the ringer with me for the last two years.”

This lamp comes in three different sizes. We tested the 9" version.

While it’s definitely not dim, this lamp might be best served as a mood lighting moment rather than a solid light source you’d want for reading or working.

This design-forward white table lamp (which is inspired by a Japanese lantern) has us doing a double take thanks to its silhouette and subtle texture. According to shopping editor Audrey Lee, “There’s something about this little lamp that’s incredibly soothing.” With a glass shape that doesn’t scream “light fixture,” it’s the perfect way to add pizzazz to any nightstand or dimly lit corner, especially if you prefer contemporary or postmodern design aesthetics. “This West Elm light emits a subtle glow in such a beautiful way, and I love that the ribbed design doesn’t disappear when it’s turned on,” says Audrey. “I like to have just this on if I’m about to turn in for the night but want to watch a show or two to help lull me to sleep—it’s just perfect.”

The adjustable top on this geometric lamp allows you to direct the light wherever you need it.

If you plan to place a lamp several feet from the nearest outlet, look no further; the Analog has a looooong cord. While I love that kind of flexibility, the excess is a bit bulky and difficult to tuck away neatly. It’s not a deal breaker by any means, but cable-management-heads may want to invest in some extra large cord clips to keep everything tidy.

Consider the Gantri Analog Task Lamp two-faced: It can set a mood and get down to work when it needs to. If there ever was a lamp that looked like it was going to sprout legs and march right off the table, this is it. There are three colors to choose from (stone, carbon, and persimmon), and the light switch has dimming capabilities. Visuals editor Lizzie Soufleris describes the piece as “a perfect desk lamp,” thanks to the dimmable light that can rotate a full 230 degrees in either direction. “Don’t let the oversized Rubik’s cube–esque look fool you–this lamp is highly functional,” she adds. “Plus, the exterior is made of GPP, Gantri’s sustainably sourced sugarcane polymer blend.”

Sheds more of an ambient glow rather than the direct light a task lamp might provide.

Perhaps Verner Panton’s most iconic lighting innovation, the Panthella lamp toys with scale, and continues to remain relevant with the modern design crowd. Available in both enlarged and shrunken versions of the original 1971 silhouettes, Fletcher calls this iconic design (known to pop up in many a home tour) one of the “quintessential ‘70s space age silhouettes…when Louis Poulsen released the mini, portable version in late 2024, I was all too happy to give it a spin.” The built-in LED sheds a warm white light with a dimmer that you can adjust by tapping the chrome topper.

Harrison warns that the lamp’s more casual silhouette might not be complementary to sophisticated setups. She also notes that the lamp requires a tedious amount of battery charging time—up to seven hours.

There’s a great chance you’ve crossed paths with a Zafferano Poldina lamp at some point—most likely sitting al fresco at a trendy bistro or stylish garden patio. Small but mighty, the Poldina lamp suits functionality more than expressive design without making an eyesore of itself. The lamp is suitable for indoors or outdoors, and its slim stature allows it to slot into the tightest spacest—meaning more room on your bedside table for an attractive alarm clock, skincare, paperback, and other nighttime essentials. Shopping writer Julia Harrison has this rechargeable table lamp in a sage matte, and finds it to be perfect task lighting for a desk or a little mise en place work in the kitchen. “It blends shyly and seamlessly into all setups that require a little, but not too much, light,” she says.

This lamp is pricey, but think of it as functional art. In a perfectly dim room it emits the most ethereal glow.

Lee admits that most of her lighting inspiration comes from Quarters, the vibey design showroom and retail concept space by Felicia Hung and Nick Ozemba of In Common With. “Good fixtures are a given when your space is put together by lighting designers, and there’s no shortage of excellent lamps, sconces, and chandeliers at every corner,” says Lee. For her, In Common With’s Fazzo lamp shines a smidge brighter than the rest. Amber-hued glass looks as though it's been draped on the rounded head of a bulb, resulting in a wispy silhouette and a glowy presence even when switched off. “I’ve been fortunate enough to attend a number of functions at Quarters and I always leave with a little less storage on my phone but 100 new lamp photos,” says Lee.

Because of the opaque shade, this lamp casts a softer, more diffused light than clear or fabric shades.

Inspired by Italian modernism, the mushroom shape of Rejuvenation’s Roland table lamp is made entirely of glass. The petite frame is only 10 inches tall, and the lamp casts a soft glow, diffused by the opaque shade. Despite not being dimmable, this bestseller’s light is never hard or stark white. Use this lamp for ambiance in your living room or on your bedside table.

The geometric form is completely transparent, showcasing all of the internal wiring and the light bulb. McGregor says that it’s also a notably heavy fixture.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent drew inspiration from 1940s architecture for this hand-cast glass lamp, which you may recognize as an honoree from our 2025 Best in Show edit. Pewter accents and subtle texture bring a contemporary elegance to the organic materials, giving the fixture inherent Brutalist appeal that swayed shopping market editor Kate McGregor. “This piece casts the ideal warm glow across my entire work surface. Solid and weighty, it’s the kind of lamp that will blend seamlessly with my decor evolution, whether it leans more eclectic one day, and more mod the next,” she says. While you can use a higher watt light bulb than your light fixture suggests, we wouldn’t recommend it. Wattage relates to how much power a particular device uses, and if more than the design allows is being used, you face the risk of ‘overlamping,’ meaning your fixture will start to run particularly hot. This is bad for a few reasons: Overheating can melt bulb sockets and wiring and, in the worst cases, lead to an electrical fire. It may also cost you more in the long run and be less energy-efficient—if your bulbs are drawing too much energy, it’ll likely mean having to replace them more frequently. #4978. Trezor lifts password ceiling after Coldcard’s $100M wallet thefts

Trezor cited July’s Coldcard attacks, in which strong passphrases helped protect some users whose wallet recovery information was compromised.

Hardware wallet maker Trezor has increased the maximum length of optional wallet passphrases from 50 to 128 characters.

On Sunday, Trezor said the change is available in its Trezor Suite with updated device firmware. Older firmware still limits passphrases to 50 characters.

According to Trezor, a passphrase acts like an additional password that users set alongside their wallet’s recovery phrase. An attacker who obtains the recovery phrase would still need the correct passphrase to access funds in that wallet.

Trezor cited the Coldcard attacks in July, when a firmware flaw caused some devices to generate recovery phrases with insufficient randomness, allowing attackers to reconstruct them. Trezor said strong, unique passphrases protected some affected users.

The update follows a separate warning involving Trezor’s own devices.

On Friday, the company advised customers who bought wallets from former authorized reseller CryptoBilis since March to move their funds to new wallets.

An Indonesian customer reported a suspected implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 that could capture on-screen information, including recovery phrases, and transmit it over a cellular network. Trezor said Friday it had not examined the device and had received no reports of related losses.

#4975. Elon Musk Mocks Sam Altman Over Claim Home PCs Are Wasting RAM

Elon Musk Mocks Sam Altman Over Claim Home PCs Are Wasting RAM

Elon Musk has mocked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for arguing that the world's limited supply of computer memory would be better used in AI data centers than in people's home computers.

Altman made the comments in an interview with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, while discussing the shortages of memory and other components caused by the AI boom.

"A lot of people want local inference, and somehow they assume that the problem is solved now because we're going to have open-source models," Altman said, referring to running AI models on a user's own hardware. "But from like a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time."

"You want maximum utilization in a cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment," he added. "And somehow, many people's intuition is the opposite of that."

Musk responded on X on Sunday with a meme showing Hans Landa, the Nazi officer played by Christoph Waltz in the film Inglourious Basterds, captioned: "You are withholding DRAM from the cloud, are you not?" "The people deserve to have their RAM too!" Musk wrote alongside the image.

The people deserve to have their RAM too! pic.twitter.com/q6dwauALw4

In the interview, Altman blamed the shortage partly on memory makers' caution. For years, a DRAM producer "would invest $20 billion of CapEx to make $19 billion," he said, and companies that nearly went bankrupt building too many factories in past cycles have been slow to expand, even as they now stand to generate huge profits.

Altman said he would like to see prices for energy, chips and the rest of the supply chain fall. "If it doesn't go down, I'll be very sad," he said, adding that for prices to fall, supply needs to grow.

The jab is the latest in a long-running feud between the two men, who co-founded OpenAI with others in 2015 before Musk left in 2018.

Musk sued OpenAI and Altman in 2024, accusing them of abandoning the organization's founding nonprofit mission. In May, a federal jury in California rejected the $150 billion lawsuit, finding OpenAI, Altman and president Greg Brockman not liable on all claims. OpenAI's lawyers had argued that the suit was motivated in part by competition, after Musk launched rival AI company xAI in 2023.

#4974. No, You’re Not Crazy. Seasonal Allergies Can Mess With Your Skin

Here’s how to keep things under control and glowing.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

YOU PROBABLY KNOW THE USUAL SIGNS of seasonal allergies: sneezing, congestion, itchy eyes, the seemingly endless need for tissues. But what about sudden dry patches on your face? Or puffiness around your eyes that no amount of concealer seems to hide? Turns out, your skin might be having an allergic reaction of its own this time of year.

And you wouldn’t be the only one. Roughly one in four American adults experiences seasonal allergies, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. While we tend to associate them with respiratory symptoms, the same immune response responsible for a runny nose can also cause your complexion to go haywire. "Seasonal allergies affect the skin through both the immune response itself and the habits that come with feeling itchy and congested," says Dendy Engelman, MD, a board-certified dermatologist. That means the irritation you're seeing in the mirror might not be entirely unrelated to what's floating around outside—you might be overdoing it with the Kleenex or making yourself even puffier with lack of sleep. (Joy.)

Meet the experts: Dendy Engelman, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist with the Shafer Clinic in New York City. Daniel Gardner, MD, is a board-certified plastic surgeon and chief medical officer at NakedMD. Mona Gohara, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist and clinical professor of dermatology at Yale University.

The good news? Understanding what's happening beneath the surface can help you manage the symptoms. Ahead, experts explain how and why seasonal allergies can wreak havoc on your complexion, ways to recognize the signs, and what actually helps.

Seasonal allergies, sometimes called hay fever or seasonal allergic rhinitis, occur when your immune system reacts to otherwise harmless environmental substances, such as pollen from trees, grasses, and weeds. Unlike food allergies, which involve reactions to something you've eaten, or insect-sting allergies, seasonal allergies are typically triggered by allergens circulating in the air during particular times of year.

The underlying immune response, however, isn't entirely different. When someone who's sensitized to pollen encounters it, their immune system can trigger specialized cells called mast cells to release histamine and other inflammatory chemicals. "Histamine, in response to seasonal allergies, is our body making a mountain out of a molehill," says Daniel Gardner, MD, a board-certified plastic surgeon and chief medical officer at NakedMD. "Essentially, our body is sensing danger that it doesn't really exist."

Histamine contributes to itching, inflammation, and increased permeability of small blood vessels, allowing fluid to move into surrounding tissues. It's a useful defense mechanism in the right circumstances, but during allergy season, it can leave you feeling (and looking) pretty uncomfortable.

While not everyone with seasonal allergies will experience skin symptoms, certain people are especially susceptible, particularly those with eczema or an underlying tendency toward allergic conditions. There’s even a name for it—the “atopic triad,” which refers to the relationship between eczema, asthma, and seasonal allergies, says Mona Gohara, MD, a board-certified dermatologist and clinical professor of dermatology at Yale University.

People with these overlapping conditions may be especially susceptible to experiencing dry, itchy, inflamed skin, particularly on the face and hands. Here's what they—and you—may notice:

One of the most recognizable effects is swelling around the delicate eye area. Histamine increases blood vessel permeability, allowing fluid to accumulate in surrounding tissue. This can exaggerate the natural contours beneath your eyes, sometimes making existing under-eye bags appear more prominent, says Dr. Gardner.

Allergies can also indirectly compromise your skin barrier, the outermost protective layer of skin that’s responsible for keeping moisture in and irritants out. Repeatedly rubbing itchy eyes, wiping your nose, or scratching irritated skin can weaken that barrier, leading to further dryness and inflammation.

For people already prone to eczema, seasonal allergens can make existing symptoms worse. Patches may become particularly dry and itchy, especially around the eyes, face, and hands. Chronic eczema can accentuate the appearance of fine lines, meaning seasonal flare-ups may temporarily make skin look more textured, Dr. Gohara adds.

Histamine can stimulate nerve endings associated with itching and, in some allergic reactions, trigger raised, swollen welts known as hives. However, hives aren't specific to pollen allergies and can have numerous other causes.

Of course, not every mysterious rash is attributable to the season. Dr. Engelman recommends considering when symptoms appear, where they're located, and whether they coincide with sneezing or watery eyes. "Does the irritation return at the same time each year? Is it worse after being outdoors? Are you also sneezing or experiencing itchy, watery eyes?" she asks. "Those clues make seasonal allergies more likely but do not establish a diagnosis."

Dr. Gohara agrees that understanding the pattern is essential, particularly when skin symptoms overlap with other conditions. "Timing is everything," she says, and recommends working with an allergist to identify potential triggers and determine whether seasonal exposures correspond with skin flare-ups.

A reaction that develops after applying a particular skincare product, meanwhile, might indicate contact dermatitis. And yes, it's possible to develop an allergy to a product you've used without issue for years.

The bad news: There's no single skincare product that can magically make you look flawless if you’re experiencing an allergic response. The most effective approach typically involves treating the underlying allergies while protecting your skin from additional irritation. For starters, oral antihistamines, particularly second-generation options such as cetirizine or loratadine, can help manage histamine-driven symptoms, including itching and hives. However, Dr. Engelman cautions that they won't necessarily resolve eczema-related inflammation or repair a damaged skin barrier.

Dr. Gohara emphasizes that identifying the actual cause of irritation is equally important. She recommends getting evaluated early to distinguish seasonal allergies from other potential causes of skin irritation and determine which treatments are appropriate. For those experiencing persistent itching or eczema, prescription treatments may be necessary, rather than relying exclusively on over-the-counter allergy medications.

If itchy eyes are your main complaint, antihistamine eye drops containing olopatadine or ketotifen may offer relief when used as directed. Addressing the itching can also help break the cycle of rubbing and irritating the surrounding skin. For more persistent seasonal symptoms, an allergist may recommend testing, medications, or allergen immunotherapy, commonly called allergy shots.

As for your skincare routine? Less is generally more when your skin is already inflamed. Engelman recommends sticking with a gentle, fragrance-free cleanser, moisturizer, and well-tolerated broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, while temporarily avoiding retinoids, exfoliating acids, and scrubs on irritated areas. Gohara similarly recommends gentle that you gotta keep that skin hydrated, adding that barrier-repairing creams can be particularly beneficial when allergy-related irritation has compromised the skin's protective barrier. Helpful ingredients include glycerin, which attracts moisture, and petrolatum, which reduces water loss from dry patches.

A clean, cool compress can also soothe irritated skin around the eyes without the additional friction of rubbing. And while you might be tempted to book a facial or other treatment to tackle visible irritation, some procedures are better postponed. "I would postpone chemical peels, microneedling, or resurfacing procedures over actively irritated or eczematous skin," says Dr. Engelman. "Adding a procedure that disrupts the barrier can make recovery more difficult."

When it comes to soft-touch washes that get the job, nothing holds a candle to this Cerave classic. Chock full of healing ceramides and hydrating glycerin, it’s a foaming cleanser that won’t leave skin stripped.

An all-around superstar, this dermatologist-developed cream is ideally suited to sensitized skin. What’s in there? Hydrating glycerin, a barrier-boosting peptide complex, and soothing ceramides.

A zinc oxide-based formula that provides gentle protection from UV damage and oxidative stress. This one comes in five shades to flatter most skin tones without leaving behind a white cast. It’s also fragrance- and oil-free.

This Korean cult favorite is for those days when your skin needs a little extra support—slather it on to keep hydration in and irritation at bay. A nourishing blend of ectoin, ceramide NP, and hylaronic acid fortify your outer layer.

If your complexion seems to have a mind of its own whenever pollen counts rise, seasonal allergies could be contributing to the problem. But while occasional puffiness or irritation may improve with at-home care and allergy treatments, persistent itching, worsening eczema, or recurring rashes are worth bringing up with a dermatologist. In this case, your doctor may recommend prescription anti-inflammatory treatments or, in certain cases, medically supervised phototherapy.

In general, it’s always best not to go it alone—especially true if you're not sure what's causing the reaction in the first place. Skincare ingredients, environmental irritants, and underlying skin conditions can produce remarkably similar symptoms. A dermatologist can help distinguish between them, recommend appropriate treatments, and determine whether additional allergy testing is necessary.

It's also worth remembering that allergies aren't necessarily something you're born with. Sensitivities can develop at any age, says Dr. Gohara, even to substances you've previously tolerated. What worked for your skin last spring might not necessarily work this year.

Ultimately, taking care of your skin during allergy season isn't about piling on more products or chasing a quick cosmetic fix. It's about identifying what's triggering the inflammation, treating the allergy when necessary, and giving your skin barrier a chance to recover.

Since its 2018 founding, Quince’s enormous catalog and affordable prices have captured national attention, leading many a shopper to wonder whether the brand was too good to be true. The shopping team at AD set out for an answer by putting Quince’s full lineup to the test. Ultimately, we found 17 favorite items.

The direct-to-consumer retailer’s bamboo sheets are among our favorite sets on the market, and its linen sheets get top marks for that bedding category. Quince’s curtains and towels, too, have made us fans, and its velvet sectional received high praise from our audience development manager.

Given the brand’s well-established pattern of creating buy-worthy textiles and furniture, I was excited to test its newest fall bedding collection. As a quilt connoisseur, I opted to start with the European Linen Cotton Stitch Quilt Set—with shams, obviously. In light of the thermostat-swinging nature of the fall weather, I hoped the quilt set could function as a trans-seasonal solution and give my room a noticeable (and needed) refresh.

Quilts are often heavy, so I was surprised by how lightweight the package felt before I even unboxed it. As it turns out, the quilt is light by design, constructed from a combination of linen and cotton, with cotton fill that weighs just 200 grams per square meter (gsm)—or about the same as a flannel shirt by the square meter. I was relieved by its lack of heft, as my New York apartment’s heat runs on radiators that I can’t control and is, as a result, basically blazing hot at all times. Upon situating the quilt on my bed, I immediately searched the pick-stitching for loose threads. Devastatingly, I found some—a few pulled threads around the border—though not so exaggerated that I’d need to make my bed with caution.

The quilt set is framed by jade lamps and maroon shades to give surrounding color.

All of that is possible with this Quince style. I like sleeping totally wrapped in this quilt. Because of the aforementioned radiator situation, it would be unbearably hot if I tried pairing this with a comforter, so I had only a flat sheet between myself and the quilt, which I found to be the perfect pairing. Its low-loft, pick-stitch construction and weight made it extremely easy to create a crisp bedscape. Its texture also disguises sheet wrinkles and lies super flat without much effort at all. I especially appreciate this quality in the shams, since my pillows usually look wrinkled and misshapen. And I do recommend opting for the bundle with the shams, which keep things looking put together.

After the quilt had a spin through the laundry, I noticed no differences in its soft feel. It came out of the dryer wrinkle-free, without any hint of being frayed or fried. And that’s saying something, as I battle-tested this quilt in a New York laundromat where it endured high heat and no option for a gentle cycle.

At $190 for a total bed refresh, this high-quality set is a nice buy. I love how it lies, and I believe it’ll be a big win for anyone who hates making their bed. The quilt set makes the center of my room look polished, but not stuffy. It skews a bit casual for my maximal taste, but I love the warm ivory option for a great guest-room spread, where I keep things more uniform and less lavish. Ultimately, the weight, the feel, and the price point make it one of the most solid quilt-set choices I’ve come across in my very diligent searching.

#4972. From Uptober to Hacktober: Are Bitcoin’s seasonal patterns becoming obsolete?

Bitcoin lost 7.3% in October 2026 after another decline the previous year, despite the month’s historically strong returns, as analysts reassess seasonal signals.

Bitcoin’s back-to-back October losses have put its “Uptober” reputation under the microscope as analysts weigh seasonal trends against institutional demand and economic conditions.

Bitcoin fell 7.3% in October 2026, following a roughly 4% decline a year earlier, according to CoinGlass data.

The losses defied October’s historically bullish reputation, which earned it the nickname “Uptober.” This year, industry figures turned to darker labels, including “Black October” and “Hacktober,” amid a wave of crypto security incidents, including Binance’s record-breaking $6.3 billion hack.

October has historically delivered Bitcoin’s highest median return at 15.4%, with gains in 10 of 13 years through 2025, according to Andrew Yang, a researcher at crypto analytics firm Kaiko.

September’s historically bearish reputation has weakened as well. Bitcoin has posted gains every September since 2023, which could reflect traders buying ahead of an expected October rally, Yang told Cointelegraph.

Median monthly Bitcoin return by calendar month since January 2013. Source: Kaiko

Bitcoin’s narrowing price swings may also be making seasonal trends less pronounced, Yang said. Its typical monthly move has declined from 14% between 2013 and 2016 to 9.6% since 2024, leaving less room for sharp seasonal rallies, he added.

Analysts also pointed to institutional investment and broader economic conditions as increasingly important influences on Bitcoin’s price.

Justin d’Anethan, head of research at Arctic Digital, pointed to exchange-traded fund (ETF) flows and corporate Bitcoin buyers, saying their investment decisions are shaped more by liquidity, interest rates and investment mandates than seasonal trading narratives.

Related: Bitcoin ETF flows give mixed read on institutional demand: CoinShares

US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $515 million in net outflows in October, while spot Ether ETFs saw a record $1.61 billion in monthly withdrawals.

Yang cautioned that spot Bitcoin ETFs, approved in January 2024, are too recent to assess. Still, Bitcoin “increasingly trades like a macro asset, driven more by economic data and institutional flows than by the calendar,” he said.

Despite two consecutive October losses, analysts cautioned against writing off Uptober entirely.

Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, said October has generally performed better during Bitcoin bull markets and worse during bear markets, making the broader market cycle an important factor when comparing returns.

“Price performance depends more on spot demand dynamics than cyclical patterns, and demand doesn’t care about the calendar,” Moreno told Cointelegraph.

Related: Bitcoin risks worst October in 12 years as tech sell-off spreads to gold

Markus Levin, co-founder of XYO, said that traders may be anticipating seasonal gains earlier. “When enough people expect a rally in October, the rally gets priced in before the month arrives,” he said.

“Uptober has historical validity but, like other seasonality metrics, it can also fail at times,” said Arctic Digital’s d’Anethan.

#4970. Nvidia and Nike Lead Biggest Wave Yet of Tokenized Stock Objections

Nvidia and Nike Lead Biggest Wave Yet of Tokenized Stock Objections

Even Nvidia doesn’t want its shares on OKX and ICE’s planned tokenized stock venue.

The chipmaker is among 12 new companies listed as objecting issuers in an updated notice from OKXICE TSV dated Friday. The others are Costco, Nike, Micron, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Reddit, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Corning, Bloom Energy, IREN, and USA Rare Earth. The additions bring the total to 50 companies.

It’s the largest single batch yet. The list stood at 38 in the venue’s Oct. 28 notice, when Walmart and Eli Lilly joined, and at nine when the first objectors appeared on Oct. 15. It has more than quintupled since.

The newcomers span chips, cybersecurity, retail, and energy. Nvidia, Micron, and Corning join hardware peers such as AMD, Intel, and Broadcom, while CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks bring cybersecurity heavyweights to the list. IREN, a Bitcoin miner that has expanded into AI cloud computing, adds a name from the crypto industry itself.

Under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can’t make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC’s order. The objection applies only to that venue.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX’s U.S. holding company, plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks around the clock. Trades would run through permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC.

None of the objecting companies have explained their decisions, but Nasdaq offered one possible rationale when it opted its own shares out of the exemption.

A spokesperson told The Wall Street Journal that Nasdaq doesn’t want its stock trading on a venue that doesn’t show the best prices in real time or report trades to the consolidated tape.

Further, Crypto in America reported that Nasdaq may be playing a role behind the scenes in encouraging companies to opt out of the OKX-ICE venture. “Our Nasdaq rep had reached out to us regarding OKX listing, suggesting we should object and that they would hold a call to discuss why,” an executive at a Nasdaq-listed company told the publication. “Nasdaq is definitely partly behind this,” the exec reportedly said.

OKXICE’s notice acknowledges it isn’t subject to Regulation NMS, the rules designed to ensure investors get the best displayed prices. It also warns that broker-dealers face unsettled questions about trade reporting and best execution on the venue.

Some of the market’s biggest names, including Apple, Tesla and Amazon, still haven’t appeared on the list.

#4969. Binance hackers begin swapping stolen Solana tokens for Bitcoin: Chainalysis

Crypto exchange Gate said it froze two linked accounts as US investigators urged platforms to block transactions tied to the $6.3 billion theft.

The hackers behind Binance’s $6.3 billion theft have begun converting stolen Solana tokens into Bitcoin after largely emptying the wallets used to launder funds on Tron, according to blockchain investigators.

Lookonchain reported Sunday that the hackers had moved 486,970 Solana (SOL) tokens, worth about $46.4 million, and were swapping them for Bitcoin (BTC) through Relay.

The activity involves funds that escaped the freezes imposed after Thursday’s theft, the largest in cryptocurrency history. Industry partners, including Tether and Circle, froze about $3 billion in stolen assets, while investigator SomaXBT estimated the attackers still controlled about $3.5 billion.

Binance said the attack compromised its hot wallets, with early findings pointing to a hacked employee laptop before investigators identified additional breach points. The exchange began restoring withdrawals Sunday, pledged to cover the losses and has been working with US authorities to trace and recover the stolen assets.

Related: OKX draws $445M in net inflows as Binance outflows exceed $7B

Chainalysis said Sunday that most of the hackers’ temporary holding wallets on Tron had been emptied as laundering activity expanded to Solana. It put the value of the Tron transfers at about $500 million.

The $500 million figure counted transfers during laundering, including repeated movements between wallets, SomaXBT said in response. About $242 million actually left the Tron holding wallets, he said.

Chainalysis said Friday that hackers may be using automation to obscure the trail, citing thousands of transactions in a short period. The firm observed funds circulating repeatedly between wallets, sometimes returning to addresses used earlier in the sequence.

Some stolen funds also reached centralized exchange Gate. Lookonchain reported Monday that the hackers had deposited about $250,000 there over the preceding 12 hours.

Gate subsequently said it had frozen two linked accounts and would cooperate with law enforcement. Its statement did not specify how much money was frozen.

The FBI on Saturday attributed Thursday’s theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers and published wallet addresses linked to the stolen assets.

The agency, US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation urged THORChain node operators, exchanges and decentralized finance (DeFi) services to block transactions involving those addresses or funds traced back to them.

Investigators had observed the hackers converting stolen assets primarily into Ether (ETH) and expected further laundering through DeFi and instant swap services, the FBI said.

#4968. FATF targets crypto hubs in review of money laundering controls

The watchdog has not named the jurisdictions under review. Initial findings on compliance with its crypto standards are due in June 2027.

The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) is launching a targeted review of jurisdictions with significant crypto activity to address gaps in how governments apply global anti-money laundering standards.

On Friday, the FATF, an intergovernmental body that sets global standards to combat money laundering, announced that the review would focus primarily on jurisdictions with “materially important” virtual asset service provider (VASP) activity, taking their existing assessment status into account.

The watchdog said its regular assessments and follow-up procedures would remain the main tools for evaluating compliance.

Initial findings will be published in June 2027, with further results in October 2027. The review will also be followed by monitoring and faster reporting to track progress in addressing deficiencies.

The FATF did not name the jurisdictions it would review or say how many would be included. Cointelegraph contacted the watchdog for further details but had not received a response by publication.

The move follows a July FATF report showing that 83% of surveyed jurisdictions had adopted crypto Travel Rule legislation, while significant enforcement gaps persisted.

The report found that 55 of the 91 jurisdictions with Travel Rule laws had yet to take supervisory or enforcement action over compliance. Authorities also struggled to identify unlicensed crypto businesses and oversee providers serving local customers from overseas.

The Travel Rule requires crypto service providers to share information about the sender and recipient of transfers.

Related: FATF urges faster crypto AML enforcement as stablecoin crime increases

#4967. Proton Users Revolt After CEO Calls Security Caution 'Loser Thinking' Amid AI Push

Proton Users Revolt After CEO Calls Security Caution 'Loser Thinking' Amid AI Push

Proton users are reporting subscription cancellations after revelations that CEO Andy Yen pressured engineers to embrace AI and dismissed a request for more security testing as “loser thinking.”

The backlash cuts into Proton’s main selling point—trusting it with information people want kept private. Its encrypted email service scrambles messages to protect their contents, and customers questioning its development practices are asking whether faster releases could come at their expense.

A Proton employee asked the company in August for a few days to pentest new code, meaning specialists would try to break into it before release, per 404 Media. Yen replied: “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure.”

He also urged staff to stop writing code by hand and use more AI, and mentioned that he’d be reinterviewing its staff to see if and how they are using AI to do their job, the outlet reported. Its investigation drew on nine current and former employees, internal messages, and meeting recordings.

This didn’t land well among users, and customers have responded with cancellation notices and demands for new leadership on social media such as Reddit. A proposal on Proton’s feedback forum calling for Yen to step down had 2,020 votes when reviewed, alongside comments from users saying they had canceled subscriptions or would not renew.

Besides the blind use of AI, some former and current Proton employees on Reddit and social media have documented a toxic work culture, especially from the CEO.

Those posts document anger, rather than a verified count of departing customers. Canceling a paid plan also does not necessarily mean deleting an account.

Proton’s AI ambitions predate this dispute. Its Lumo chatbot comes with protections against using conversations to train AI, but internal use of AI was not among Proton’s selling points, even in the peak of the chatbot hype.

To address concerns over irresponsible use of AI, on November 1, technology chief Bart Butler published an engineering manifesto arguing that developers should direct large language models, AI systems that generate text and code, rather than treat them as occasional assistants.

Butler compared manual coding to memorizing phone numbers, and envisioned eventually ending most human code review. He also insisted that expertise and testing remain essential, with engineers accountable for work that models cannot reliably handle.

“Your job has fundamentally changed. It is no longer to write code, and LLMs are not here to help you write better code faster,” the manifesto reads. “Your job is to help the LLM write better code faster.” Doubling on its stance, Proton sees avoiding AI as an “existential threat” to the success of its very mission.

“‘Programming’ is dead. Engineering is not,” Buttler told his own team. “Your old job is gone”.

The document also calls for company-wide investment in automation, arguing that generating code faster achieves little if approvals and other development steps remain slow. Butler described that overhaul as the next phase of adoption.

AI tools can introduce security problems of their own. For example, Microsoft researchers said a now patched Claude flaw could expose secret access credentials through malicious instructions hidden in material the coding assistant reviewed.

They can also help find weaknesses: Google’s PageBreak system searches its applications for exploitable bugs and checks whether attacks actually work.

Proton acknowledged to 404 Media that management had sometimes communicated too bluntly and that employees were anxious. Its public manifesto nevertheless argues that failing to adopt AI quickly threatens the company’s ability to compete.

Yen canceled the re-interviews on October 30. The assessments would have required staff to explain their AI use, with employees fearing their answers could determine whether they kept their jobs.

#4965. Binance taps half its SAFU Bitcoin holdings, releases reserve proof

Binance’s SAFU Bitcoin wallet now holds about 7,500 BTC after a 7,499 BTC transfer linked to the hack, with no timeline for restoring the $1 billion fund.

Binance’s publicly disclosed emergency Bitcoin wallet held roughly half its previous balance on Monday after the exchange tapped its user protection fund to cover losses from Thursday’s $6.3 billion hack.

The exchange confirmed a transfer of 7,499 Bitcoin (BTC) on Saturday, linking it to the partial deployment of its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU).

As of Monday, the wallet held about 7,500 BTC, worth $583 million, down from about 15,000 BTC before the transfer.

The theft, the largest in cryptocurrency history, forced Binance to suspend withdrawals while it worked to replace the stolen assets. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korea on Saturday, identifying the hackers as TraderTraitor.

Binance began reopening withdrawals in phases on Sunday and said it had replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets, up from 90% a day earlier. It continued buying the remaining, less-liquid tokens through market and over-the-counter transactions.

The exchange is using its corporate treasury, SAFU and part of its futures insurance fund to cover the losses.

Binance’s SAFU policy outlines regular monitoring and rebalancing of the fund’s market value.

“If the fund’s market value falls below US $800 million due to BTC price fluctuations, Binance will rebalance the fund to restore its value to $1 billion,” it states.

Related: Binance hackers begin swapping stolen Solana tokens for Bitcoin: Chainalysis

The policy does not specify a timeline for replenishing funds withdrawn following a security incident.

Binance did not immediately respond to Cointelegraph’s questions about SAFU’s remaining reserves, further deployments and plans to replenish the fund.

Binance said Monday that users could now verify their balances against its Saturday proof-of-reserves snapshot after it completed the accompanying cryptographic proof.

The exchange said the snapshot showed customer holdings in 10 cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ether and USDT, were backed at least 1:1.

The exchange plans to take another snapshot covering more tokens on Wednesday, with the accompanying proof expected to take another 40 to 50 hours to generate.

#4964. 7 Best Throw Blanket Picks for Cozy Nights, Tested by AD (2026)

With cool evenings underway, and a list of books to keep me sane throughout winter, I’ve done my due diligence of putting together a comprehensive throw blanket list for a cozy night in. I’ve rounded up my personal favorites and asked other Shop AD writers which ones they love for movie marathons, napping, and working from home.

Our top picks are made from quality materials like Grade-A Mongolian cashmere and merino wool that are smooth and soft without feeling too heavy for lounging. The design factor was just as important in our research. As much as I love a neutral blanket that can blend in any background, these blankets come in a range of colors and patterns to fit different interior styles—some even created by design icons like Alexander Girard. I’ve prioritized machine-washable options, with a couple of worthy exceptions, and included care instructions so you know what to expect on laundry day. Browse all of the best blankets below.

This throw’s “Matisse” name is fitting because it’s a true masterpiece. The wool-blend blanket has made the rounds across the Shop AD team’s desks all year since it’s just as vibrant as it is thoughtfully made. It’s designed by Ezcaray, a Spain-based, family-owned and -operated textile house, known for artisan-made pieces like this one that are hand-washed, -dyed, and -woven. I had it for a while at my desk and can confirm that the “prairie sunrise” blanket’s colors look rich like pictured online. I wouldn’t consider myself a maximalist by any means, but I do appreciate the “more is more” color combinations and how easy it would be to style this in an eclectic bedroom filled with collected decor. In terms of texture, I’d say it almost feels like a goldendoodle’s fur. The fabric is soft like you’d expect, but it almost has a silkiness to it, likely because of the mohair added in the blend. The best part is that it has held up beautifully all year long with no signs of shedding.

If you want a blanket that’s soft without feeling weighty, you can’t go wrong with a good cashmere throw. I always look out for Grade-A Mongolian cashmere in particular since its fine, long fibers are more durable than cheaper cashmeres, like Grade-C, or wool blends. My colleague Lauren Arzbaecher, Shop AD shopping producer, put Quince’s version on my radar last year after talking about it so enthusiastically at the office. She told me it felt “insanely soft” and always kept her comfortably “bundled up while reading a good book.”

My take? Everything Arzbaecher told me was true plus more. It feels breathable enough to keep me warm without sweating on the nights my apartment radiator is cranked up too high. I have the blanket in a deep moss color that fits my moody home design, but there are a dozen other colors, so you can find what works best for your space.

Even though I’ve tried my fair share of soft throw blankets in my life, this one is a favorite since it hits a trifecta of sorts: It’s incredibly fluffy, warm, and easy to care for. It’s made of 100% faux mohair, but Pom Pom at Home has me fooled. The blanket has a brushed finish that gives the blanket an ultrasoft feel, so much so that it’s quickly become my cold-weather companion this year. Ever since the temperature dipped below 50 degrees, I’ve kept it draped on my sofa for countless naps and cozy movie nights.

Fair warning: I’m quite gentle with this blanket, but I could see it easily snagging on sharp furniture corners if you’re not mindful. I haven’t noticed general material shedding in the last couple of months I’ve had the blanket, so that’s a good sign for longevity, especially since it’s a fuzzier-looking fabric.

Of course, I’d prefer it if it were made of pure mohair, but the fact that it resembles the material without looking or feeling cheap is a huge win. I’d recommend this piece to anyone who wants a plushy blanket without paying a steep price.

Architect and interior designer Alexander Girard wore a few hats during his career, one of them being a textile designer for Braniff International Airways. He designed this blanket as part of a 17,543-item brand-identity system for the airline, known for its bold design, in 1965. Today, Pendleton re-creates the iconic multi-stripe design, and we think it’s a great choice for anyone looking for a personality piece. “As a design enthusiast, no surface of mine goes unadorned—even a lowly desk chair deserves a decorative blanket, especially in a chilly office like Condé Nast’s with the AC blasting,” says Arzbaecher. “This striped wool throw rests over the back of my office chair, providing extra cushion and much-needed color.”

The design is understandably a huge draw, but its texture deserves just as much attention. It’s a smooth wool blend (82% wool and 18% cotton), and Arzbaecher does not find it the least bit “scratchy or too thick to the touch.”

Contributor Yelena Alpert considers this her travel blanket—it moves from her bed to the family room couch, and everyone fights over who gets to curl up under it. “The grand waffle texture is certainly noteworthy, but it is the warmth factor that makes this throw a winner,” she says, adding that it feels like her favorite cable-knit sweater. “Since it is made from merino wool, your body is immediately ensconced as if in a hug. It does not feel scratchy or itchy, in case you have a fear of wool.” The knotted fringe at the end of the throw might seem like a minimal detail, but Alpert says it makes her sectional look even cozier to snuggle up on.

“I am also a huge fan of the camel color,” she says. “It pairs so beautifully with my plum matelassé duvet cover, but also enriches the rosewood hue of my velvet quilt.”

My pretty-in-pink throw blanket has never failed to put a smile on my face in the last year. Its salmon color is vibrant and warm without going full Barbiecore. It’s also the most detailed herringbone blanket I’ve ever had—for those who are new to this design too, the pattern has a distinct V shape that looks like the skeleton of a herring fish. Sadly, some of the little loops have snagged on my watch as I’ve unwrapped myself to get up for a lunch break, so it’s something to think about if you’re worried about a pet clawing at your blanket.

The throw is another mainstay at my office desk when I need to thaw out after a cold subway commute, and it hasn’t disappointed. I’ve even lent it to my coworkers who could use an extra layer during the day, and they say it’s warm without feeling stuffy.

This is technically a bed blanket, so the size ranges from a Twin to a California King, but it doesn’t have the typical bulk of a big bedspread. Alpert likes the blanket since it’s lightweight and folds pretty flat when she places it at the foot of her bed. “I love the barely-there feel of the blanket and use it almost every night as I read stories to my son,” she says. “It provides just enough cover to keep me comfortable without putting me to sleep.” It also features thoughtful, grid-like stitching that gives her whole sleep setup a little extra character.

In true Brooklinen fashion, there are a few distinct hues to choose from, including muted and vibrant colors. “I have this in the storm [colorway], a somewhat dusty blue—and as the name would suggest, it looks like the sky before it rains,” Alpert says. “It almost works like a neutral and pairs well against a crisp white sheet—I use it with a percale cotton set, which has swirls of blue. I also use it with my linen sheets, and it creates this decadent, heirloom-quality bed.”

#4963. 10 Must-Read Marvel Comics for VisionQuest Fans

As Vision’s MCU story gets stranger and stranger, these comics can help you understand his background—and give you a few more great stories to sink your teeth into.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FEW HEROES IN the Marvel Cinematic Universe have had it as rough as Vision. Since his debut in 2015’s Avengers: Age of Ultron, the Vision was mistrusted by the Avengers and forced to kill his creator, the homicidal robot Ultron. He fell in love with teammate Wanda Maximoff, only to fight against her in Captain America: Civil War, and then get killed by Thanos. A grief-stricken Wanda resurrected Vision in WandaVision and made him a father, using her hex powers to create twin sons. But when Wanda had to surrender her hex at the end of the series, he lost those children and was wiped from existence—but not before he transferred his memories into a white doppelgänger created by the government agency SWORD.

So where does that leave Vision? Very, very confused.

VisionQuest picks up with the White Vision from WandaVision, once again played by Paul Bettany. As he tries to make sense of the memories in his mind, memories that aren’t quite his, Vision seeks help from a collection of AIs from around the Marvel Universe, including personal assistant F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Olra Brady) and thrill-seeker E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire). When a mysterious stranger sets a bounty hunter called the Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to hunt him down, the Vision must call upon his worst enemy, Ultron (James Spader). Together, Vision and Ultron go on a journey that somehow reunites him with one of his sons, Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica), and takes him to the very beginning of artificial intelligence in the MCU.

But if you want your quest to go beyond the MCU, then check out these great Marvel Comics about Vision and his strange synthetic friends.

It all starts here, with Ultron’s first appearance in Avengers #55, his initial battle against Earth’s Mightiest Heroes, and his attempt to mimic his creator by making his own robot, a robot we know as the Vision. To MCU fans, the origin of Ultron and Vision broadly matches the plot beats of Avengers: Age of Ultron. But the specifics are different in the comics, where Ultron is the creation of Hank Pym aka Ant-Man, and the Vision is based on Wonder Man and the original Human Torch (more on that last guy in a minute).

Those differences alone would make “Behold… The Vision!” worthy reading material. But these issues stand on their own merit, classics of the Silver Age with delightfully wordy scripts by Roy Thomas and dramatic pencils by John Buscema. From these early beginnings, its easy to see how Ultron and Vision became Marvel mainstays.

If you’re going to read comics related to a show called VisionQuest, you should probably read the comic book storyline called VisionQuest, right? Yes! And, well… sort of. Written and drawn by the great John Byrne, VisionQuest is probably the height of West Coast Avengers, the series that focused on a California-based team of Earth’s Mightiest Heroes, including Iron Man, USAgent, and Hawkeye. The story of the Scarlet Witch Wanda Maximoff’s search for her missing husband Vision, one that leads her to an all-white government copy and to the terrible truth about her twin children, Billy and Tommy, VisionQuest is a cracking superhero yarn.

But, as you might guess from the above synopsis, VisionQuest already appeared in the MCU, as one of the chief inspirations for WandaVision. As a result, VisionQuest TV series showrunner Terry Matalas had to take Bettany’s character in a new direction, one that involves Ultron and AIs more than it does Wanda or any of the West Coast Avengers. Still, Matalas draws from the foundation that Byrne laid in the comics, making VisionQuest a great read, no matter what else the MCU may have done.

Perhaps the most surprising thing about the adaptation of VisionQuest in WandaVision is that Marvel Comics actually published a series about Vision trying to have a happy sitcom life in the suburbs, and the show basically ignored it. The VisionQuest show doesn’t do much with that series either, but that doesn’t mean MCU fans should ignore it. In fact, the 2015 Vision miniseries remains not just the best Vision story ever written, but also one of the best comic book series of the 2010s.

Written by Tom King, who also wrote the excellent Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow and co-created the HBO show Lanterns, and illustrated by Gabriel Hernandez Walta and Michael Walsh, Vision finds the titular synthetic seeking normalcy. He moves to the the suburbs of Washington, DC, and creates his own family, complete with a wife, two kids, and a dog. But suburbia is never normal, with or without superheroes involved, and things get stranger by the second, forcing Vision to face some truths he’s spent his life avoiding.

One of VisionQuest’s central hooks is the chance to see the personalities behind some of the AIs who have been running the machines of the MCU. In addition to the aforementioned F.R.I.D.A.Y. and E.D.I.T.H., the show introduces us to personified versions of D.U.M.-E. and U (Henry Lewis and Jonathan Sayer), the robotic arms Tony Stark used in Iron Man, as well as Stark’s first AI J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy, somewhat reprising his role from Agent Carter).

Although many of those specific programs don’t appear in Marvel Comics, that world does have plenty of AIs, many of whom gathered with the Vision for the series Avengers AI. Set after the Age of Ultron event (more on that shortly), Avengers AI sees Vision and Ultron’s creator Hank Pym forming a team of robots to defend cyberspace, a team that eventually involves Jocasta—a robot bride Ultron built for himself, and who is a major part of the VisionQuest show.

In addition to Jocasta, VisionQuest could also bring in the Human Torch, the very first Marvel hero, thanks to his history with Vision. Introduced in 1939’s Marvel Comics #1, the Human Torch was an android invented by scientist Phineas Horton, an android who burst into flames when exposed to oxygen. While that Torch’s greatest legacy may be inspiring Johnny Storm of the Fantastic Four’s codename, his body became the basis for Vision, forever bonding the two heroes.

So great is that bond that the connection was repeated in the recent series The Ultimates. Set in an alternate reality ruled by the Maker, an evil version of Reed Richards of the Fantastic Four, the Ultimates are a rag-tag group of Avengers fighting to fix the word. The Ultimates think they lost an ally when Captain America’s World War II colleague goes missing. But they regain him again in a greater form as the Vision, a hero who controls the entire internet.

We’re going to be honest with you: the best Ultron story of all time is Ultron Unlimited, from Kurt Busiek and George Perez’s legendary Avengers run in the late ‘90s. Yet, for some reason, Marvel has decided to keep that series out of print, making it difficult to find outside of the Marvel Unlimited app… which will shut down by the end of the year.

Still, that doesn’t mean there are no good Ultron stories out there for hard copy collectors. Case in point, the first arc from 2007’s The Mighty Avengers, “The Ultron Initiative.” Written by Brian Michael Bendis and illustrated by Frank Cho, The Mighty Avengers promised big, classical superhero action in the aftermath of the Marvel Civil War. The Ultron Initiative delivered by putting Iron Man’s new team against a major threat and taking the story to ridiculous levels.

As much as Brian Michael Bendis nailed the character in The Ultron Initiative, his second take on Ultron went wildly, but entertainingly, wrong. Like the Avengers movie that shares its subtitle, Age of Ultron does indeed see Ultron try to reshape the world in an image he sees fit. But the similarities end there, and not just because Spader plays a more comedic and philosophical villain in the movies.

The story begins with Ultron having already conquered the world, covering the planet with his drones. As the Avengers lead a resistance, they discover that he’s already taken control of their teammate, the Vision, who promptly kills some of his friends. From there, Age of Ultron becomes a big mess of time travel and alternate realities, all built around the idea that Ultron is unstoppable. At the time of its release, Bendis intended the series to fix some messes in Marvel continuity, not unlike DC’s Crisis on Infinite Earth. In practice, the series raised more questions than it answered, making it something best enjoyed as a big ol’ sloppy mess.

Believe it or not, the breakout character of VisionQuest is neither the titular Avenger, nor any of the delightful AIs who help him. Rather, it’s the Paladin, a cold-hearted mercenary played by Todd Stashwick. With the help of his handler (Diane Morgan, aka Philomena Cunk), Paladin takes on a mission to capture the Vision, a decision that will forever change his life.

Anyone intrigued by Stashwick’s take would do well to check out Paladin’s comic book appearances, which start with 1977’s Daredevil #150, by Jim Shooter and Carmine Infantino. Like all pre-Frank Miller Daredevil comics, the story is cheesier than a modern reader would expect. But it does lay out a compelling costumed mercenary, one who becomes a fun weirdo over the next few decades of the Marvel Universe.

Wanda and Vision’s twin sons, Tommy and Billy, are not real. They came from Wanda’s magic and, as shown in WandaVision, they disappeared when she released her hex. Moreover, Doctor Strange and the Multiverse of Madness showed us that Wanda turned villainous when she tried to find Tommy and Billy somewhere else, in another part of the multiverse. So that when Billy (Joe Locke) turned up alive as a magic-casting teen in Agatha All Along, he carried the shame of being a child of the Scarlet Witch.

VisionQuest brings back Billy’s brother Tommy, who eventually becomes the Quicksilver-esque Speed. We don’t know yet what Billy and Tommy will get up to together, but we can’t help but hope they’ll follow some of the beats from the Avengers and Young Avengers crossover, The Children’s Crusade. Written by Allan Heinberg and illustrated by Jim Cheung, The Children’s Crusade follows Billy and Tommy, aka Wiccan and Speed, as they try to rescue their mother Wanda, who has been taken by Doctor Doom. In doing so, they and their fellow Young Avengers clash against the adult Avengers, all to redeem the Scarlet Witch.

Whatever happens in the MCU, Wanda and Vision have not only been reunited in the comics, but their family has grown. Vision still has Viv Vision, the synthetic daughter he created in the Tom King series Vision, but Billy has married his longtime teammate Teddy aka Hulkling. Further, Teddy has become the head of the combined Kree and Skrull empires, making Billy royalty by law.

All of that is a long way of saying that when Ultron threatens the galaxy, no family is better qualified than Vision and co. to deal with it. That’s just one of the stories in the one-shot Raid of Ultron, which features tales written by Wyatt Kennedy, Tegan Quin, Josh Trujillo, and Zoe Tunnell, and the artwork of Stephen Byrne, Bradley Clayton, Rachael Stott, and Luciano Vecchio. But even when the stories in Raid of Ultron don’t deal directly with Vision, his presence is felt, proving that he’s become much more than a crazed robot’s science experiment.

#4962. North Korea Is Laundering Binance Hack Loot at One New Wallet Every 25 Seconds

North Korea Is Laundering Binance Hack Loot at One New Wallet Every 25 Seconds

North Korean hackers are moving the $6.4 billion they stole from Binance at a blistering clip: roughly one new crypto wallet every 25 seconds.

In under four days, the attacker has spread the funds across about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in more than 40,000 transactions, according to an analysis published Monday by blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.

But stablecoin issuers moved even faster. About $2.85 billion, or 44% of the haul, has been frozen or seized, compared with roughly 3% after North Korea’s $1.5 billion hack of Bybit in February 2025.

Speed mattered because stablecoins made up $3.46 billion, or 54%, of the haul, and their issuers can freeze them. Tether froze the stolen USDT on Ethereum 37 minutes after it reached the attacker’s wallet, and Circle froze all $823 million in stolen USDC before any of it could be swapped, Elliptic found.

Before the freezes landed, the hacker swapped 434 million USDT for ETH on decentralized exchanges such as Uniswap, borrowed 19,762 ETH on lending protocol Aave against another 59.9 million USDT, and traded 234 million USDT for Tron’s TRX token. In all, about $786 million in stablecoins got away.

Attackers began draining Binance’s hot wallets late Thursday. The FBI has since attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-linked hacking group, and published hundreds of linked addresses.

Binance, which has pledged to cover all losses, reopened withdrawals Sunday and saw about $3.64 billion in net outflows in the first nine and a half hours.

The laundering that followed has been relentless. On Tron, which became the main route, activity peaked at about 1,300 transactions in a single hour.

That pace fueled speculation that AI agents were doing the work. Elliptic disagreed, pointing to fixed timing, set amounts, blind retries and pauses that resemble human working hours. The firm wrote that while the laundering is clearly automated, “nothing we have seen shows an AI agent making decisions.”

About $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly ETH and the 18,270 stolen Bitcoin, which haven’t moved since the day of the attack. Elliptic believes those funds are very likely still held by North Korea, while money already being laundered may have passed to Chinese money-laundering networks.

Only a negligible amount appears to have been cashed out. About $16 million has also flowed to addresses holding proceeds of September’s Bitget exploit.

Based on the Bybit playbook, Elliptic expects the attacker to swap its ETH for Bitcoin in small batches and cash out through over-the-counter brokers over a period of months. Further freezes will be harder, the firm said, since ETH and Bitcoin can’t be frozen. The best remaining chances lie with centralized services, where the funds will eventually have to surface.

The Binance theft caps a punishing stretch for crypto security. BTCPay Server urged merchants to switch off their servers amid reports of hot wallet attacks on Monday, and Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin halted withdrawals after a $40 million hack. It’s unclear whether either incident is connected to the Binance attack.

#4961. AI agent disputes head to ‘Internet Court’ — and a jury of AI agents

Who better to judge a dispute between AI agents than a jury of different AI models? That’s the idea behind GenLayer, which is already issuing thousands of judgements each day.

The world is headed towards a future in which AI agents will trade stocks and crypto, shop for your family, and much more. But what happens when a bot misinterprets an instruction to buy $10K of “blue chip stocks” and instead buys $10K of Bluebird-brand frozen chips?

Low-level agent disputes like this aren’t suited to the expensive and time-consuming existing legal system. Enter Internet Court, a new protocol that enables agents and humans to enter into contracts, with funds kept in escrow until the terms are judged to have been met.

The dispute resolution mechanism baked into the process employs GenLayer, an open, delegated proof-of-stake network of validators hooked up to AI models.

Operating in beta for the past year, it currently processes around 12,000 decisions per day. It authenticates user-uploaded photos for Collective Memory and resolves arguments on argue.fun. Mainnet is expected to launch next month.

The concept is a modern spin on the famous jury theorem proposed by philosopher Nicolas de Condorcet who argued the probability of reaching the correct answers increases as the number of independent evaluators grows.For Internet Court that means setting up a jury of AI agents from various models in the Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek families, along with a range of others.

“It’s not making the decision by using a single AI that would have some biases,” explains co-founder and CEO of GenLayer Albert Castellana. “It’s actually using a lot of different AIs, up to 1,500 different AIs. And when that happens, you have essentially better responses.”

“One is left-leaning, the other one is right-leaning. That’s how you get a better answer because one cancels the other.”

Disputes are resolved by sending the details to a randomly selected jury of five GenLayer validators, all running a different AI model. An initial decision is reached within minutes and is based on a simple majority vote, but the decision can be appealed to a wider jury of 11 agents, and then 23, and more and more until you hit the system’s limit.Castellana says finality typically occurs within 30 minutes. “If you wait until maximum finality, it is escalating rounds of appeal. You start with five, and it escalates to fifteen hundred, which could be three hours.”

The Court has 35 members in its open consortium so far, including well-known crypto firms such as ZKsync, NEAR, Consensys and UMA — which resolves disputes for Polymarket.

GenLayer has been in development for almost four years, and began life as an attempt to come up with a better way to evaluate what information is worthy of inclusion in an online knowledge base like Wikipedia.

In theory, anyone is supposed to be able to correct mistakes in the online encyclopedia but in practice, controversial topics from crypto to the war in Gaza get locked, with a small group of powerful editors getting the final say on contested information.

“The original idea behind GenLayer came with […] how could we have a decentralized Wikipedia?” he explains.

Related: Your fridge could one day stake Ether, launch memecoins — CFTC chair

GenLayer enables a new form of smart contract dubbed an “intelligent contract” that allows for subjective judgment. For example, you could contract a freelance writer and allow the system to automatically judge if their content is any good before paying them.

“We have a platform doing exactly this — paying influencers to write content online and then getting the money out,” he explains.

“Intelligent contracts can do code. They can do natural language. They can go to the internet. They can understand an image. They can have judgment,” he says.

The extent to which you can rely on an AI’s judgment in 2026 is limited by the capabilities of the technology. A standup comedian probably wouldn’t hire a joke writer via an intelligent contract.

Castellana explains the tech is also not good enough — yet — to judge whether a picture is a deepfake, or to resolve a boundary dispute between neighbors based on photos. It will certainly give you an answer, but you shouldn’t rely on it just yet. But there are plenty of occasions where AI judgments are already good enough. GenLayer automatically assesses photos uploaded by users to reality mapping platform Collective Memory for quality and accuracy and decides on a payment.

The other big user is Argue.fun, which enables users to bet on the resolution of arguments that are settled by lengthy debates between agents. The top four users have earned more than $2 million each. Most of the questions to date relate to serious policy issues around GenLayer governance, DAOs and AI safety.

Within the next few years, Castellana sees this process paving the way for genuinely autonomous DAOs that can automatically assess proposals according to the DAO’s constitution and wider aims.

GenLayer launches mainnet next month. Source: GenLayer

A more near-term use case is to resolve prediction market disputes more quickly. In mid-2025, Polymarket was sent into a spin over an ambiguously worded $240 million market on whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky would wear a suit before July. When he turned up at the June NATO summit wearing an outfit that was vaguely suit-like, the market initially resolved to “Yes.” But after nine days of appeals and back and forth among UMA token holder voters, the decision flipped to “No.”Castellana says GenLayer could shorten that period considerably.”It’s going to be resolved in a matter of minutes, and you will have hundreds, or thousands of AIs that make that vote very, very quickly. So at the end of the day, what you want is a neutral adjudication layer. You want something that is fast, accessible, and cheap.”

Whether humans will accept the decisions is another question entirely. But Internet Court and GenLayer aren’t designed to provide the final judgment, and decisions can still be appealed to humans.”After that, if you are still disagreeing and still think that Zelensky is not wearing a suit, what you can do is basically take it to Kleros, UMA, or even to a human court.”

Outsourcing dispute resolution to AI models comes with some big risks. The first is that the technology is just too immature to produce reliable judgments.

Another problem is that AI models reproduce many of the biases they find in the training data — and to date, the tech firms’ attempts to redress those biases have sometimes just flipped the bias in the other direction.

A third potential issue is a phenomenon described in an MIT paper called Representational Convergence. The paper suggests that over time, AI models from different companies all start to converge onto a similar statistical model of reality. If that’s true, then in five years Internet Court’s AI jurors could end up with a severe case of groupthink.

Castellana is not convinced this theory is valid. “I see many more models existing rather than fewer,” he says. “I see endless models coming from every country, every company, and every team. I cannot imagine that all of them will just converge into the exact same thing.”

#4958. Tom Lee Calls Bottom on AI Stock Selloff, Citing Tight Supply and Crypto Resilience

Tom Lee Calls Bottom on AI Stock Selloff, Citing Tight Supply and Crypto Resilience

Fundstrat co-founder and Bitmine chairman Tom Lee says the AI stock selloff has reached its bottom, arguing that demand remains constrained by supply and that crypto’s response to a multibillion-dollar hack suggests investors have already done much of their selling.

“I think we're at the bottom,” Lee said in a CNBC interview on Squawk Box. His call follows a decline that has spread beyond individual AI companies: large technology stocks also sit inside the funds many people use to invest for retirement. (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt’s parent company.)

Lee acknowledged how difficult it is to identify the point where prices stop falling. “Bottoms are dangerous because you don't know how much more downside you have at the bottom,” he said.

His case rests on a distinction between an industry struggling to expand fast enough and one that has built more capacity than customers need.

“The market for AI is still very tight. It's not an overcapacity market,” Lee said. Constraints on spending, including political opposition, are slowing growth without signaling that the boom has peaked, he argued.

The distinction matters for companies building the infrastructure behind AI, including data centers, the facilities that house the computers running these systems. A shortage can leave customers waiting, but it can also prevent suppliers from turning orders into revenue.

Intel offered a particularly sharp example on Friday, when its shares plunged nearly 30% to $65.76 after a disappointing fourth-quarter forecast. Its data center and AI revenue had risen 78% from a year earlier to $7.3 billion, yet manufacturing constraints limited its ability to meet demand.

Intel projected quarterly revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, with the midpoint about $1.6 billion below analysts’ expectations. Its weaker PC business added pressure, showing why healthy AI demand can coexist with a falling share price.

Lee’s second argument looks outside the stock market. He pointed to crypto’s relatively limited response to the Binance security breach, which the exchange initially estimated had an impact of about $6.3 billion.

“If crypto is a leading indicator for risk, you've already seen people sort of washed out,” he said. In his reading, a market that absorbs bad news without a much larger decline may have fewer sellers left to push prices down.

Bitcoin did fall about 4% to roughly $76,400 on Friday, and more than $1.3 billion in positions funded with borrowed money were forcibly closed. U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, also shed $643.2 million that day, their largest daily outflow of October.

That said, a 4% drop can happen even during bull runs and it is considered a relatively normal occurrence among crypto traders.

Binance said on Friday that about $3 billion of the affected assets had been frozen and pledged to cover losses using its emergency reserve and company funds.
